nodes.note: The field is the negative gradient of potential: $$E = -\frac{dV}{dr}$$. Equipotential surfaces are always perpendicular to field lines.

nodes.label: Ring on Its Axis
nodes.note: For a ring of mass $M$ and radius $R$, an axial point at $x$ sees $$V = -\frac{GM}{\sqrt{R^2 + x^2}}$$. The axial field peaks at $x = R/\sqrt{2}$ and vanishes at the centre.

nodes.label: Solid Sphere: Interior Field
nodes.note: Only the enclosed mass matters inside a uniform sphere: $$E = \frac{G M r}{R^3} = \frac{4}{3}\pi G \rho\, r$$. Hence $E$ grows linearly from zero at the centre.

nodes.label: Potential at the Centre
nodes.note: Integrating the interior field gives $$V_{center} = -\frac{3}{2}\frac{GM}{R} = \frac{3}{2}V_{surface}$$. It is the deepest (most negative) point of the sphere.

nodes.label: Neutral Point Between Two Masses
nodes.note: Between two attracting masses there is one point of zero field: $$\frac{M_1}{x^2} = \frac{M_2}{(D - x)^2} \Rightarrow x = \frac{\sqrt{M_1}}{\sqrt{M_1} + \sqrt{M_2}}D$$. Potential there is negative and is never a maximum of force.

nodes.label: Variation of g
nodes.note: How the measured value of g shifts with altitude, depth, latitude, and planetary shape. Sign errors in these approximations are a classic trap.

nodes.label: Altitude Dependence
nodes.note: Above the surface gravity falls as $$g_h = \frac{g}{(1 + h/R)^2} \approx g\left(1 - \frac{2h}{R}\right)$$ for $h \ll R$. The fractional drop is $2h/R$.

nodes.label: Depth Dependence
nodes.note: Below the surface only the inner sphere pulls, so $$g_d = g\left(1 - \frac{d}{R}\right)$$, falling linearly to zero at the centre. A depth of $d = 2h$ matches the gravity loss at height $h$.

nodes.label: Rotation and Latitude
nodes.note: Centrifugal effect of spin reduces effective gravity: $$g_{eff} = g - \omega^2 R \cos^2\theta$$. The reduction is maximal at the equator and zero at the poles.

nodes.label: Shape of the Earth
nodes.note: The oblate earth has $R_{eq} > R_{pole}$, and since $$g \propto \frac{1}{R^2}$$, polar gravity exceeds equatorial gravity. Combined with rotation, $g_{pole} - g_{eq} \approx 0.034\ \text{m/s}^2$.

nodes.label: Altitude vs Depth Rate
nodes.note: Differentiating the two approximations gives $$\left|\frac{dg_h}{dh}\right| = \frac{2g}{R} = 2\left|\frac{dg_d}{dd}\right|$$. Gravity weakens twice as fast with height as with depth.

nodes.label: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: Energetics of assemblies of masses and the minimum speed needed to leave a planet forever. Energy bookkeeping replaces force bookkeeping here.

nodes.label: Two-Body Potential Energy
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: The mutual potential energy of masses $M$ and $m$ is $$U = -\frac{GMm}{r}$$. Lifting a body by $h$ from the surface costs $$\Delta U = \frac{mgh}{1 + h/R} \approx mgh$$ for $h \ll R$.

nodes.label: Gravitational Self-Energy
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: The work to assemble a uniform sphere from dispersed matter is $$U_{self} = -\frac{3}{5}\frac{GM^2}{R}$$, while a thin shell needs $$-\frac{GM^2}{2R}$$. Self-energy sets the magnitude of binding in stars and planets.

nodes.label: Escape Speed
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: Zero total energy at infinity defines the escape speed: $$v_e = \sqrt{\frac{2GM}{R}} = \sqrt{2gR} \approx 11.2\ \text{km/s}$$. It is independent of projectile mass and launch direction unless the path intersects the planet.

nodes.label: Escape Variants
nodes.group: Potential Energy, Self-Energy and Escape Speed
nodes.note: From height $h$ or at speed boosted at some point, use energy conservation with $$\frac{1}{2}v^2 - \frac{GM}{r} = const$$. On the Moon $v_e \approx 2.4\ \text{km/s}$, explaining its airless surface.

nodes.label: Kepler's Laws
nodes.note: The three empirical laws of planetary motion, all derivable from Newtonian gravity. Expect one derivation-based question every year.

nodes.label: First Law: Orbits
nodes.note: Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at a focus: $$a = \frac{r_p + r_a}{2},\quad r_p = a(1 - e),\quad r_a = a(1 + e)$$. The semi-major axis $a$ alone fixes the energy of the orbit.

nodes.label: Second Law: Equal Areas
nodes.note: Areal velocity is constant because angular momentum is conserved: $$\frac{dA}{dt} = \frac{L}{2m} = \frac{1}{2}r^2\omega = const$$. Hence planets move fastest at perihelion: $$\frac{v_p}{v_a} = \frac{r_a}{r_p}$$.

nodes.label: Third Law: Harmonic Law
nodes.note: The period squared scales with the cube of the semi-major axis: $$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3$$. For two planets around the same star, $T_1^2/T_2^2 = a_1^3/a_2^3$.

nodes.label: Satellite Motion
nodes.note: Circular orbits, orbital energy, geostationary and polar satellites, and classification by launch speed. Pure centripetal-gravity balance.

nodes.label: Orbital Speed
nodes.note: Gravity supplies the centripetal force: $$\frac{mv_0^2}{r} = \frac{GMm}{r^2} \Rightarrow v_0 = \sqrt{\frac{GM}{r}}$$. A near-Earth satellite needs $v_0 \approx 7.9\ \text{km/s}$.

nodes.label: Orbital Period
nodes.note: The period follows from $T = 2\pi r/v_0$: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{(R + h)^3}{GM}}$$. A near-Earth orbit takes about $84$ minutes.

nodes.label: Satellite Energy
nodes.note: Summing kinetic and potential terms gives a negative total: $$E = -\frac{GMm}{2r} = -K = \frac{U}{2}$$. The binding energy that must be supplied to free the satellite is $|E|$.

nodes.label: Binding Energy
nodes.note: Binding energy equals the energy needed to reach infinity with zero speed: $$BE = \frac{GMm}{2r}$$. It grows as the orbit shrinks, so low orbits are more tightly bound.

nodes.label: Geostationary Satellite
nodes.note: A geostationary orbit matches Earth's spin: $T = 86400\ \text{s}$, equatorial plane, prograde motion. Its radius is $$r = \left(\frac{GMT^2}{4\pi^2}\right)^{1/3} \approx 6.6 R \Rightarrow h \approx 36000\ \text{km}$$.

nodes.label: Trajectory vs Launch Speed
nodes.note: Launch speed selects the conic: $v < v_0$ sub-orbital ellipse, $v = v_0$ circle, $v_0 < v < v_e$ ellipse, $v = v_e$ parabola, $v > v_e$ hyperbola. Only the last two escape: $$v_{\infty} = \sqrt{v^2 - v_e^2}$$.

nodes.label: Binary Star Systems
nodes.note: Two stars orbiting their common centre of mass, reducible to a one-body problem via reduced mass. A direct application of Kepler's third law.

nodes.label: Centre of Mass
nodes.note: Both stars circle the common CM with $$m_1 r_1 = m_2 r_2,\quad r_1 + r_2 = d$$. The lighter star moves on the larger orbit.

nodes.label: Reduced Mass
nodes.note: The two-body motion is equivalent to one body of mass $$\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$$ orbiting a fixed centre. All one-body formulas apply with $\mu$ in place of $m$.

nodes.label: Period of the Binary
nodes.note: Balancing gravity against centripetal force for each star gives $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{d^3}{G(m_1 + m_2)}}$$. Kinetic energies split inversely with mass: $K_1/K_2 = m_2/m_1$.

nodes.label: Kinematics
nodes.note: Rectilinear motion, projectile motion, and relative motion. JEE tests calculus-based kinematics, graph interpretation, and vector decomposition.

nodes.label: Rectilinear Motion Fundamentals
nodes.note: One-dimensional motion along a straight line: distance, displacement, velocity, and acceleration.

nodes.label: Distance vs Displacement
nodes.note: Distance is the total path length (scalar); displacement is the straight-line vector from initial to final position. The fundamental inequality is $$s \ge |\Delta \vec{r}|$$, with equality only for straight unidirectional motion.

nodes.label: Equality Condition
nodes.note: Distance equals displacement magnitude if and only if the particle moves along a strictly straight line without ever reversing direction.

nodes.label: Speed and Velocity
nodes.note: Average velocity is displacement over time; average speed is total distance over time. Always $$v_{\text{avg, scalar}} \ge |\vec{v}_{\text{avg}}|$$.

nodes.label: Average Velocity
nodes.note: $$\vec{v}_{\text{avg}} = \frac{\Delta \vec{r}}{\Delta t} = \frac{\vec{r}_f - \vec{r}_i}{t_f - t_i}$$. Instantaneous velocity is the limit as $$\Delta t \to 0$$: $$\vec{v} = \frac{d\vec{r}}{dt}$$.

nodes.label: Mean Speed Theorems
nodes.note: For equal distance segments, $$v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{2 v_1 v_2}{v_1 + v_2}$$ (harmonic mean). For equal time intervals, $$v_{\text{avg}} = \frac{v_1 + v_2}{2}$$ (arithmetic mean).

nodes.label: Acceleration and Calculus
nodes.note: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: $$\vec{a} = \frac{d\vec{v}}{dt} = \frac{d^2\vec{r}}{dt^2}$$. In one dimension, $$a = \frac{dv}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}$$ by the chain rule.

nodes.label: Differential Form
nodes.note: The spatial form $$a = v \frac{dv}{dx}$$ is derived from $$\frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}$$. It is essential for position-dependent acceleration problems.

nodes.label: Uniformly Accelerated Motion
nodes.note: Motion with constant acceleration: the master equations, vertical free fall, and graph calculus.

nodes.label: Equations of Motion
nodes.note: The three master equations for constant acceleration: $$v = u + at$$, $$s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2 = \frac{u+v}{2}t$$, and $$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$$.

nodes.label: Displacement in nth Second
nodes.note: The displacement in the $$n$$-th second is $$s_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n-1)$$. This is not the total distance in $$n$$ seconds.

nodes.label: Vertical Motion Under Gravity
nodes.note: Taking upward as positive, a body projected up with speed $$u$$ decelerates at $$g$$. Time of ascent equals time of descent: $$t_a = t_d = \frac{u}{g}$$.

nodes.label: Maximum Height
nodes.note: At maximum height $$v = 0$$, so $$H_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{2g}$$. The body returns to projection level with the same speed $$u$$.

nodes.label: Dual Time Conjugates
nodes.note: For any height $$h < H_{\max}$$, the two times $$t_1$$ (ascending) and $$t_2$$ (descending) satisfy $$t_1 + t_2 = \frac{2u}{g}$$ and $$t_1 t_2 = \frac{2h}{g}$$.

nodes.label: Kinematics Graphs
nodes.note: The slope of an $$x$$-t graph gives velocity; the slope of a $$v$$-t graph gives acceleration. The area under a $$v$$-t graph gives signed displacement.

nodes.label: Area Under v-t Graph
nodes.note: The algebraic area under a $$v$$-t curve yields displacement ($$\Delta x = \int v\,dt$$). For total distance, take the absolute value: $$s = \int |v|\,dt$$.

nodes.label: Area Under a-x Graph
nodes.note: The area under an acceleration-displacement curve gives $$\int a\,dx = \frac{v_f^2 - v_i^2}{2}$$. This is the work-energy relation per unit mass.

nodes.label: Galileo's Law of Odd Numbers
nodes.note: For a particle starting from rest under uniform acceleration, displacements in consecutive equal time intervals follow the ratio $$s_1 : s_2 : s_3 : \dots = 1 : 3 : 5 : \dots : (2n-1)$$.

nodes.label: Stopping Distance
nodes.note: Total stopping distance combines reaction distance and braking distance: $$D_{\text{stop}} = u t_r + \frac{u^2}{2a}$$. Reaction distance scales linearly with speed; braking distance scales quadratically.

nodes.label: Projectile Motion
nodes.note: Two-dimensional motion under uniform gravity: independence of horizontal and vertical components, flight parameters, and trajectory geometry.

nodes.label: Independence of Motion
nodes.note: A projectile's horizontal motion is uniform ($$v_x = u\cos\theta = \text{const}$$) and vertical motion is uniformly accelerated ($$a_y = -g$$). The two components are completely independent.

nodes.label: Flight Parameters
nodes.note: Time of flight, maximum height, and range are the three canonical flight parameters for ground-to-ground projectiles.

nodes.label: Time of Flight
nodes.note: Setting $$y = 0$$ gives $$T = \frac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$$. Time of ascent equals time of descent: $$t_a = t_d = \frac{T}{2}$$.

nodes.label: Height and Range
nodes.note: Maximum height is $$H_{\max} = \frac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$$ and horizontal range is $$R = \frac{u^2\sin 2\theta}{g}$$. The geometric link is $$\tan\theta = \frac{4H_{\max}}{R}$$.

nodes.label: Maximum Range
nodes.note: For fixed $$u$$, range is maximized at $$\theta = 45^\circ$$ giving $$R_{\max} = \frac{u^2}{g}$$. The height at maximum range is $$H = \frac{u^2}{4g}$$.

nodes.label: Equation of Trajectory
nodes.note: Eliminating time from the kinematic equations yields the parabolic trajectory $$y = x\tan\theta - \frac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$$.

nodes.label: Factorized Range Form
nodes.note: The trajectory can be rewritten as $$y = x\tan\theta\left(1 - \frac{x}{R}\right)$$. This form is ideal for clearance problems over walls and obstacles.

nodes.label: Complementary Angles
nodes.note: Two projectiles launched at the same speed $$u$$ at angles $$\theta$$ and $$90^\circ - \theta$$ have identical ranges: $$R(\theta) = R(90^\circ - \theta)$$.

nodes.label: Inter-Trajectory Relations
nodes.note: For complementary angles, $$T_1 T_2 = \frac{2R}{g}$$ and $$R = 4\sqrt{H_1 H_2}$$. Also $$H_1 + H_2 = \frac{u^2}{2g}$$ and $$\frac{T_1}{T_2} = \tan\theta$$.

nodes.label: Radius of Curvature
nodes.note: The radius of curvature at any point on the trajectory is $$\rho = \frac{v^2}{a_\perp}$$ where $$a_\perp$$ is the normal component of acceleration.

nodes.label: Curvature at Peak
nodes.note: At the topmost point, $$v = u\cos\theta$$ and $$a_\perp = g$$, so $$\rho_{\text{top}} = \frac{u^2\cos^2\theta}{g}$$. This is the global minimum radius of curvature.

nodes.label: Inclined Plane Ballistics
nodes.note: On an incline of angle $$\beta$$, choose axes along and perpendicular to the incline. The launch angle $$\alpha$$ is measured relative to the incline surface.

nodes.label: Optimal Launch Angles
nodes.note: Maximum range up the incline occurs at $$\alpha = 45^\circ - \frac{\beta}{2}$$ giving $$R_{\text{up,max}} = \frac{u^2}{g(1+\sin\beta)}$$. Down the incline, $$\alpha = 45^\circ + \frac{\beta}{2}$$ gives $$R_{\text{down,max}} = \frac{u^2}{g(1-\sin\beta)}$$.

nodes.label: Relative Motion
nodes.note: Frame transformations, closest approach geometry, and classic 2D relative motion problems.

nodes.label: Frame Transformations
nodes.note: Relative position, velocity, and acceleration follow vector subtraction: $$\vec{r}_{B/A} = \vec{r}_B - \vec{r}_A$$, $$\vec{v}_{B/A} = \vec{v}_B - \vec{v}_A$$, $$\vec{a}_{B/A} = \vec{a}_B - \vec{a}_A$$.

nodes.label: Two-Projectile Theorem
nodes.note: Two projectiles in flight under gravity have $$\vec{a}_{\text{rel}} = \vec{g} - \vec{g} = 0$$. Their relative motion is uniform straight-line at constant velocity $$\vec{v}_{2/1} = \vec{u}_2 - \vec{u}_1$$.

nodes.label: Closest Approach
nodes.note: The velocity of approach is $$v_{\text{app}} = -\frac{dr}{dt}$$. At closest approach, $$v_{\text{app}} = 0$$ and the relative velocity is perpendicular to the line of sight.

nodes.label: Closest Approach Geometry
nodes.note: For initial separation $$r_0$$ and relative velocity at angle $$\theta$$ to the line of sight, $$d_{\min} = r_0\sin\theta$$ and $$t_{\min} = \frac{r_0\cos\theta}{|\vec{v}_{\text{rel}}|}$$.

nodes.label: River-Boat Crossing
nodes.note: A boat crosses a river of width $$d$$ with current speed $$v_r$$ and boat speed $$u$$ relative to water. Shortest time and shortest path are different strategies.

nodes.label: Shortest Time
nodes.note: Steer perpendicular to the bank ($$\theta = 90^\circ$$): $$t_{\min} = \frac{d}{u}$$. The downstream drift is $$x = \frac{v_r d}{u}$$. Crossing time is independent of river speed.

nodes.label: Zero Drift
nodes.note: To land directly opposite, steer upstream with $$\sin\alpha = \frac{v_r}{u}$$ (requires $$u > v_r$$). The crossing time is $$t = \frac{d}{\sqrt{u^2 - v_r^2}}$$.

nodes.label: Minimum Drift When Slower
nodes.note: When $$u < v_r$$, zero drift is impossible. The minimum drift is $$x_{\min} = d\sqrt{\frac{v_r^2}{u^2} - 1}$$ achieved at $$\sin\alpha = \frac{u}{v_r}$$.

nodes.label: Rain-Man Problem
nodes.note: Rain falls with velocity $$\vec{v}_r$$ and a person moves with velocity $$\vec{v}_m$$. The apparent rain velocity is $$\vec{v}_{r/m} = \vec{v}_r - \vec{v}_m$$.

nodes.label: Umbrella Tilt
nodes.note: To stay dry, hold the umbrella opposite to the apparent rain direction. The tilt angle from vertical is $$\tan\theta = \frac{|v_{rx} + v_m|}{v_{ry}}$$. For vertical rain, $$\tan\theta = \frac{v_m}{v_r}$$.

nodes.label: Polygon Pursuit
nodes.note: $$N$$ particles at the vertices of a regular $$N$$-gon each move toward their cyclic neighbor at speed $$v$$. They spiral into the center.

nodes.label: Pursuit Time
nodes.note: The approach speed is $$v_{\text{app}} = v[1 - \cos(2\pi/N)]$$, so the meeting time is $$t_{\text{meet}} = \frac{d}{v[1 - \cos(2\pi/N)]}$$. For a triangle, $$t = \frac{2d}{3v}$$; for a square, $$t = \frac{d}{v}$$.

nodes.label: Kinetic Theory of Gases
nodes.note: Kinetic theory models a gas as point molecules in random motion, turning pressure into a statistical average: $$P = \frac{1}{3}\rho \overline{v^2}$$. Degrees of freedom then fix heat capacities.

nodes.label: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: Empirical gas laws combine into the ideal gas equation $$PV = nRT$$, with $R = 8.314\ \text{J}/\text{mol}\cdot\text{K}$.

nodes.label: Boyle's Law
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: At fixed temperature, pressure and volume are inverse: $$P \propto \frac{1}{V}, \ P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$$. The isotherm is a rectangular hyperbola on the P-V plane.

nodes.label: Charles's and Gay-Lussac's Laws
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: At fixed pressure $V \propto T$; at fixed volume $P \propto T$: $$\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}, \ \frac{P_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2}{T_2}$$. Absolute temperature in kelvin is mandatory.

nodes.label: Combined Gas Law
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: One relation covers all three variables: $$\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$$. It applies to a fixed mass of ideal gas between two equilibrium states.

nodes.label: Dalton's Law of Partial Pressures
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: Total pressure is the sum of partial pressures of non-reacting components: $$P = p_1 + p_2 + p_3 + \dots, \ p_i = \frac{n_i}{n}P$$. Moist gas questions subtract water vapour pressure.

nodes.label: Dalton Mixture Example
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: A $2\ \text{L}$ vessel holds $1\ \text{mol}$ N$_2$ and $1\ \text{mol}$ O$_2$ at $300\ \text{K}$: each partial pressure is $p_i = \frac{n_iRT}{V} \approx 12.5\ \text{atm}$, so $P \approx 25\ \text{atm}$.

nodes.label: Graham's Law of Diffusion
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: Effusion rates are inversely proportional to the square root of molar mass: $$\frac{r_1}{r_2} = \sqrt{\frac{M_2}{M_1}}$$. It explains isotopic separation of uranium hexafluoride.

nodes.label: Graham Ratio Example
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: He vs O$_2$: $$\frac{r_{He}}{r_{O_2}} = \sqrt{\frac{32}{4}} = \sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$$. Helium effuses nearly three times faster.

nodes.label: Avogadro's Hypothesis and Molar Volume
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: Equal volumes of gases at the same $T$ and $P$ contain equal molecules: at STP one mole occupies $22.4\ \text{L}$. Density then scales as $$\rho = \frac{PM}{RT}$$.

nodes.label: Open Vessel Heating
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: An open vessel at fixed $P$ and $V$ loses molecules on heating: $$\frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{T_1}{T_2}$$. The fraction expelled is $$1 - \frac{T_1}{T_2}$$.

nodes.label: Moist Gas Correction
nodes.group: Gas Laws and Equation of State
nodes.note: Gas collected over water contains water vapour: $$P_{gas} = P_{atm} - P_{water}$$. Vapour pressure of water depends only on temperature.

nodes.label: Kinetic Theory Postulates and Pressure
nodes.note: Ideal gas molecules are point masses with elastic collisions and no intermolecular forces. Pressure follows from momentum transfer: $$P = \frac{1}{3}\frac{N}{V}m\overline{v^2}$$.

nodes.label: Postulates of KTG
nodes.note: Molecules move randomly, collisions are perfectly elastic, and collision time is negligible. Between collisions the gas obeys Newtonian mechanics with pressure emerging statistically.

nodes.label: Kinetic Interpretation of Temperature
nodes.note: Average translational kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature: $$\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2} = \frac{3}{2}k_BT$$. This is why $T = 0\ \text{K}$ means zero kinetic energy.

nodes.label: Why Ideal Model Fails at High Density
nodes.note: At high pressure, finite molecular size and attractions matter. The van der Waals correction is $$\left(P + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$$.

nodes.label: Collision Frequency
nodes.note: Molecules of one species collide at rate $$Z_1 = \sqrt{2}\pi d^2 n \bar{v}$$. Total intermolecular collisions per unit volume per second scale as $$Z_{11} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\pi d^2 n^2 \bar{v}$$.

nodes.label: Molecular Speeds
nodes.note: A Maxwell-Boltzmann ensemble yields three characteristic speeds: most probable, mean, and rms. Their ranking is $$v_{mp} < \bar{v} < v_{rms}$$.

nodes.label: RMS Speed
nodes.note: Root-mean-square speed is $$v_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}} = \sqrt{\frac{3k_BT}{m}}$$. It grows as $\sqrt{T}$ and falls as $\sqrt{M}$.

nodes.label: Mean and Most Probable Speeds
nodes.note: $$\bar{v} = \sqrt{\frac{8RT}{\pi M}}, \ v_{mp} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$$. The ratio $v_{mp} : \bar{v} : v_{rms} = 1 : 1.128 : 1.225$ is a frequent JEE ask.

nodes.label: Speed Ratio Example
nodes.note: For O$_2$ at $300\ \text{K}$, $v_{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/M} \approx 483\ \text{m}/\text{s}$, while $v_{mp} \approx 395\ \text{m}/\text{s}$.

nodes.label: Maxwell-Boltzmann Distribution
nodes.note: The speed probability density is $$f(v) = 4\pi\left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_BT}\right)^{3/2} v^2 e^{-mv^2/2k_BT}$$. Higher $T$ flattens and right-shifts the curve.

nodes.label: Mean Free Path
nodes.note: Average distance between collisions is $$\lambda = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 n} = \frac{k_BT}{\sqrt{2}\,\pi d^2 P}$$. It falls as pressure rises.

nodes.label: Temperature and Molar Mass Shift
nodes.note: The most probable speed scales as $$v_{mp} = \sqrt{\frac{2RT}{M}}$$. Heating shifts the Maxwell peak right; heavier gases shift it left.

nodes.label: Degrees of Freedom and Equipartition
nodes.note: Each quadratic energy term contributes $\frac{1}{2}k_BT$ per molecule. For $f$ degrees of freedom, $$U = \frac{f}{2}nRT$$.

nodes.label: Degrees of Freedom by Gas Type
nodes.note: Monatomic gases have $f = 3$ (translation only), diatomic have $f = 5$ at ordinary temperatures (3 translational + 2 rotational), and polyatomic have $f = 6$ with vibrations active.

nodes.label: Law of Equipartition of Energy
nodes.note: Energy is shared equally among all accessible quadratic modes: $$E_{mode} = \frac{1}{2}k_BT$$ per molecule. This explains why adding rotational modes raises heat capacity.

nodes.label: Heat Capacities and Gamma
nodes.note: Molar heats satisfy $$C_P - C_V = R, \ \gamma = \frac{C_P}{C_V} = 1 + \frac{2}{f}$$. So $\gamma = 5/3$ for monatomic and $7/5$ for diatomic gases.

nodes.label: Gas Mixtures
nodes.note: Internal energy is additive: $$U = \frac{1}{2}(n_1f_1 + n_2f_2)RT$$. Effective gamma is $$\gamma_{mix} = \frac{n_1C_{P1} + n_2C_{P2}}{n_1C_{V1} + n_2C_{V2}}$$.

nodes.label: Vibrational Modes and High-Temperature Failure
nodes.note: Vibrations add 2 degrees of freedom per mode, giving $f = 7$ classically. Quantum freezing of modes explains why measured $C_V$ falls below classical predictions at low $T$.

nodes.label: Internal Energy of Ideal Gas
nodes.note: $$U = \frac{f}{2}nRT = nC_V T$$. Since $U$ depends only on $T$, any isothermal ideal-gas process has $\Delta U = 0$.

nodes.label: Speeds in Reaction and Effusion
nodes.note: Effusion rate through a small hole is $$r = \frac{P}{\sqrt{2\pi m k_B T}}$$ per unit area. It yields Graham's law on integration over the Maxwell distribution.

nodes.label: Real Gases
nodes.note: Real gases deviate from ideality, captured by the compressibility factor $$Z = \frac{PV}{nRT}$$.

nodes.label: Compressibility Factor Z
nodes.note: $Z = 1$ marks ideality; $Z < 1$ shows attraction dominance; $Z > 1$ shows repulsion/finite size. Z vs P curves at fixed $T$ are classic graph questions.

nodes.label: Z Curve Reading
nodes.note: For H$_2$ and He, $Z > 1$ at all pressures near room temperature because repulsions dominate. For CO$_2$, $Z$ dips below 1 at moderate pressures before rising.

nodes.label: Van der Waals Equation
nodes.note: $$\left(P + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT$$ with $a$ correcting attraction and $b$ correcting volume. Both constants are material-specific.

nodes.label: Critical Constants
nodes.note: At the critical point the isotherm has an inflection: $$P_c = \frac{a}{27b^2}, \ V_c = 3b, \ T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb}$$. Above $T_c$ no liquefaction is possible.

nodes.label: Boyle Temperature
nodes.note: At $T_B$ a real gas mimics ideal behavior over a wide pressure range: $$T_B = \frac{a}{Rb}$$. Below $T_B$ attractions dominate at low pressure.

nodes.label: Virial Equation of State
nodes.note: $$\frac{PV}{RT} = 1 + \frac{B(T)}{V} + \frac{C(T)}{V^2} + \dots$$. From van der Waals, $B(T) = b - a/(RT)$.

nodes.label: Liquefaction of Gases
nodes.note: A gas liquefies only below its critical temperature: $$T < T_c = \frac{8a}{27Rb}$$. Cooling plus compression along the Andrews isotherm produces the liquid phase.

nodes.label: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
nodes.group: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
nodes.note: Current creates magnetic fields, fields push moving charge, and matter answers back by magnetizing. The chain runs $$d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{l} \times \hat{r}}{r^2}$$ into forces and then into hysteresis.

nodes.label: Biot-Savart Law and Current Fields
nodes.note: Every current element contributes a field that falls as $$1/r^2$$ and curls around the wire. Integration over standard shapes gives all the results JEE asks for.

nodes.label: Biot-Savart Law
nodes.note: A current element sends out a field along the cross product of its direction and the radial vector: $$d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_0}{4\pi}\frac{I\,d\vec{l} \times \hat{r}}{r^2}$$. The constant is $$\frac{\mu_0}{4\pi} = 10^{-7}\ \text{T}\cdot\text{m/A}$$.

nodes.label: Straight Current-Carrying Conductors
nodes.note: A finite wire at perpendicular distance $$d$$ gives $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{4\pi d}(\sin\alpha_1 + \sin\alpha_2)$$ with angles measured from the foot of the perpendicular. Infinite wires double to $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi d}$$, and a semi-infinite wire gives half that.

nodes.label: Circular Arc and Loop Centre Field
nodes.note: On a circular arc only the perpendicular components survive, giving $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I \phi}{4\pi R}$$ for angle $$\phi$$. A full loop therefore has $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2R}$$ at its centre, or $$\frac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}$$ with $$N$$ turns.

nodes.label: Circular Loop on Its Axis
nodes.note: Off-axis components cancel and only the axial part remains: $$B(x) = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$$. Two coaxial coils a radius $$R$$ apart give a nearly uniform field of $$B = \frac{8\mu_0 N I}{5\sqrt{5}R}$$, the Helmholtz case.

nodes.label: Solenoid and Toroid
nodes.note: A long solenoid packs turns into a uniform interior field $$B = \mu_0 n I$$, falling to half at the end. A toroid closes the flux on itself, giving $$B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2\pi R}$$ inside and zero outside.

nodes.label: Ampere's Circuital Law
nodes.note: Ampere's law turns hard integrals into a counting of enclosed current: $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{enc}$$. It works only where symmetry makes $$B$$ constant on the loop.

nodes.label: Statement of Ampere's Law
nodes.note: The circulation of $$\vec{B}$$ around any closed path depends only on current threading it: $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{l} = \mu_0 I_{enclosed}$$. It is the magnetic counterpart of Gauss's law for charges.

nodes.label: Field Inside and Outside a Thick Conductor
nodes.note: Current spreads uniformly through a wire of radius $$R$$, so only part of it is enclosed at radius $$r < R$$. That gives $$B(r) = \frac{\mu_0 I r}{2\pi R^2}$$ inside and $$B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$$ outside, peaking at the surface.

nodes.label: Choosing an Amperian Loop
nodes.note: Pick a loop on which $$B$$ is constant and parallel to $$d\vec{l}$$, usually a circle centred on the current. Then $$B(2\pi r) = \mu_0 I_{enc}$$ solves for $$B$$ in one line.

nodes.label: Gauss's Law for Magnetism
nodes.note: Magnetic field lines have no beginning or end because isolated poles do not exist. Every closed surface therefore collects zero net flux: $$\oint \vec{B}\cdot d\vec{A} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Motion of Charged Particles
nodes.note: A magnetic force perpendicular to velocity bends motion without changing speed, so the trajectory is circular or helical. The radius is always $$r = \frac{mv}{qB}$$.

nodes.label: Lorentz Force and Zero Work
nodes.note: The full force law combines both fields: $$\vec{F} = q(\vec{E} + \vec{v} \times \vec{B})$$. Since the magnetic part is perpendicular to motion it does no work, $$W_B = 0$$, and kinetic energy stays fixed.

nodes.label: Circular Motion in a Uniform Field
nodes.note: Entering perpendicular to $$\vec{B}$$, the Lorentz force plays the centripetal role, giving $$r = \frac{mv}{qB}$$. The orbit period $$T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$$ is independent of speed, which is why cyclotrons work.

nodes.label: Helical Motion at an Angle
nodes.note: Only the perpendicular velocity component circles, while the parallel component slides undisturbed. With entry angle $$\theta$$ the pitch is $$p = v_{\parallel}T = \frac{2\pi mv\cos\theta}{qB}$$.

nodes.label: Time Spent in a Field Region
nodes.note: Inside a magnetic strip a particle turns through angle $$\theta$$ before leaving, and the turn time follows from the period. The time is $$t = \frac{m\theta}{qB}$$, independent of speed.

nodes.label: Velocity Selector
nodes.note: Crossed electric and magnetic fields can cancel exactly for one speed, letting undeflected particles through. The selected velocity is $$v = \frac{E}{B}$$, set only by the field ratio.

nodes.label: Cyclotron
nodes.note: An alternating voltage at the resonant frequency kicks the particle each half turn, while $$B$$ keeps it on a spiral. Resonance needs $$f = \frac{qB}{2\pi m}$$, and the Dee radius $$R$$ caps energy at $$K = \frac{q^2B^2R^2}{2m}$$.

nodes.label: Force and Torque on Currents
nodes.note: Summing the Lorentz force over a wire gives a macroscopic force and, for loops, a torque. The wire result is $$F = ILB\sin\theta$$.

nodes.label: Force on a Current-Carrying Wire
nodes.note: A straight segment in a field feels $$\vec{F} = I\vec{L}\times\vec{B}$$, so magnitude is $$F = ILB\sin\theta$$. The force vanishes when the wire runs parallel to the field.

nodes.label: Force Between Parallel Currents
nodes.note: Each wire sits in the other's field, so force per unit length is $$\frac{F}{L} = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$$. Currents in the same direction attract and opposite directions repel.

nodes.label: Torque on a Current Loop
nodes.note: Opposite sides of a loop push opposite ways, so the net force cancels but a couple survives: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{M} \times \vec{B}$$ with $$\tau = NIAB\sin\theta$$. This is exactly what spins a galvanometer coil.

nodes.label: Magnetic Moment and Potential Energy
nodes.note: A loop is a dipole with moment $$\vec{M} = NIA\hat{n}$$, and it aligns to lower energy: $$U = -\vec{M}\cdot\vec{B} = -MB\cos\theta$$. Stable equilibrium is at $$\theta = 0$$, unstable at $$\theta = 180^\circ$$.

nodes.label: Closed Loop in a Uniform Field
nodes.note: For any closed current loop in a uniform field the forces around the perimeter cancel exactly: $$\vec{F}_{net} = 0$$. Only a non-uniform field can translate the loop, which is how magnetic traps and dipoles behave.

nodes.label: Galvanometer and Instruments
nodes.note: A coil in a radial field converts current into deflection against a spring, and shunts or multipliers turn it into meters. Balance reads $$NIAB = C\theta$$.

nodes.label: Moving Coil Galvanometer
nodes.note: A cylindrical core makes the field radial, so torque stays at right angles to the plane of the coil. Deflecting torque then balances the restoring torque of the strip: $$NIAB = C\theta$$, giving $$I = \frac{C}{NAB}\theta$$.

nodes.label: Why the Field Is Made Radial
nodes.note: With the field always in the plane of the coil, the angle stays at 90 degrees and the scale becomes linear. Torque is then $$\tau = NIAB$$ at every deflection, independent of $$\theta$$.

nodes.label: Current and Voltage Sensitivity
nodes.note: Current sensitivity is deflection per ampere, $$S_i = \frac{NAB}{C}$$, while voltage sensitivity divides by coil resistance, $$S_v = \frac{S_i}{R_g}$$. Doubling turns doubles both $$S_i$$ and $$R_g$$, leaving $$S_v$$ unchanged.

nodes.label: Galvanometer as an Ammeter
nodes.note: A low shunt resistor diverts most current past the delicate coil. For range $$0$$ to $$I$$ the shunt is $$S = \frac{I_g R_g}{I - I_g}$$, and the finished ammeter has very low resistance.

nodes.label: Galvanometer as a Voltmeter
nodes.note: A high series resistance limits current so the meter reads potential difference across it: $$R = \frac{V}{I_g} - R_g$$. The ideal voltmeter draws nothing, meaning $$R_V \to \infty$$.

nodes.label: Earth's Magnetism
nodes.note: The Earth behaves like a huge bar magnet whose field is resolved into horizontal and vertical parts. The dip angle ties them as $$\tan\delta = \frac{B_V}{B_H}$$.

nodes.label: Magnetic Elements of the Earth
nodes.note: Declination gives the angle between geographic and magnetic meridians, and dip gives the tilt of the total field below horizontal. Components follow $$B_H = B_e\cos\delta$$ and $$B_V = B_e\sin\delta$$.

nodes.label: True and Apparent Dip
nodes.note: Dip measured outside the magnetic meridian reads low, so two perpendicular readings recover the true value. They obey $$\cot^2\delta = \cot^2\delta_1 + \cot^2\delta_2$$, with true dip the smallest possible reading.

nodes.label: Tangent Law
nodes.note: A needle under two perpendicular fields settles where their torques balance, turning angle into a field ratio. The law is $$B = B_H\tan\theta$$ for the applied field $$B$$.

nodes.label: Tangent Galvanometer
nodes.note: A vertical circular coil in the magnetic meridian adds its own field perpendicular to $$B_H$$. Combining coil field and tangent law gives $$I = \frac{2RB_H}{\mu_0 N}\tan\theta$$.

nodes.label: Vibration Magnetometer
nodes.note: A magnet displaced in the meridian oscillates about equilibrium under the restoring torque of $$B_H$$. The period is $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{MB_H}}$$, which lets moments be compared by timing.

nodes.label: Neutral Points
nodes.note: A neutral point is where the magnet's own field exactly cancels the horizontal component of Earth's field. There the net field is zero, $$B_{mag} = B_H$$, and a compass refuses to turn.

nodes.label: Magnetic Properties of Matter
nodes.note: Matter magnetizes in response to an applied field, and its susceptibility classifies it. The constitutive link is $$B = \mu_0(H + I)$$.

nodes.label: Magnetization and Permeability
nodes.note: Magnetization is magnetic moment per unit volume, $$I = \frac{M_{net}}{V}$$, and permeability measures how easily the medium supports flux. They combine as $$B = \mu_0(1 + \chi)H$$ with $$\chi = \frac{I}{H}$$.

nodes.label: Classification of Magnetic Materials
nodes.note: Diamagnets have small negative susceptibility, paramagnets small positive susceptibility, and ferromagnets enormous positive susceptibility. The values run $$-1 \le \chi < 0$$ for diamagnets, $$0 < \chi < 10^{-3}$$ for paramagnets, and $$\chi \sim 10^2$$ upward for ferromagnets.

nodes.label: Curie's Law
nodes.note: Heat jostles paramagnetic alignment, so susceptibility falls with absolute temperature: $$\chi = \frac{C}{T}$$. Above its Curie temperature a ferromagnet obeys $$\chi = \frac{C}{T - T_c}$$ instead.

nodes.label: Hysteresis Loop
nodes.note: The B versus H curve lags behind the applied field, marking saturation, residual flux, and the coercive field. Retentivity $$B_r$$ is the flux left at $$H = 0$$, and coercivity $$H_c$$ is the reverse field needed to reach $$B = 0$$.

nodes.label: Hysteresis Loss and Material Choice
nodes.note: Energy lost per cycle per unit volume equals the enclosed loop area: $$W = \oint B\,dH$$. Narrow-loop soft iron suits transformer cores at 50 Hz, while broad-loop steel with high coercivity makes permanent magnets.

nodes.label: Superconductors and Perfect Diamagnetism
nodes.note: Below its critical temperature a superconductor expels every field line from its interior. That makes it a perfect diamagnet with $$\chi = -1$$ and $$\mu_r = 0$$, so $$B = 0$$ inside.

nodes.label: Newton's Laws of Motion and Friction
nodes.group: Newton's Laws of Motion and Friction
nodes.note: The three laws of motion, pseudo forces, constraint mechanics, and friction. JEE tests FBD isolation, elevator apparent weight, Atwood machines, and two-block friction thresholds.

nodes.label: Newton's Three Laws
nodes.note: The foundational laws of dynamics: inertia, force-momentum relation, and action-reaction.

nodes.label: First Law: Inertia
nodes.note: A body continues in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an unbalanced external force: $$\sum \vec{F}_{\text{ext}} = 0 \iff \vec{a} = 0$$. This defines inertial reference frames.

nodes.label: Second Law: F = ma
nodes.note: The net force equals the rate of change of momentum: $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = \frac{d\vec{p}}{dt}$$. For constant mass, $$\vec{F}_{\text{net}} = m\vec{a}$$.

nodes.label: Impulse-Momentum Theorem
nodes.note: The impulse of a force equals the change in momentum: $$\vec{J} = \int_{t_i}^{t_f} \vec{F}\,dt = \Delta\vec{p} = \vec{p}_f - \vec{p}_i$$. The area under an $$F$$-$$t$$ curve gives impulse.

nodes.label: Third Law: Action-Reaction
nodes.note: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction: $$\vec{F}_{AB} = -\vec{F}_{BA}$$. The pair acts on two different bodies simultaneously and can never cancel.

nodes.label: Action-Reaction Properties
nodes.note: Action and reaction act on distinct bodies, are simultaneous, share the same physical nature, and are collinear. They never act on the same body and never cancel each other.

nodes.label: Pseudo Force
nodes.note: In a non-inertial frame accelerating at $$\vec{a}_0$$, a fictitious force $$\vec{F}_{\text{pseudo}} = -m\vec{a}_0$$ must be introduced. It has no reaction partner and acts through the center of mass.

nodes.label: Apparent Weight in Elevator
nodes.note: In an elevator accelerating upward at $$a$$: $$N = m(g+a)$$. Accelerating downward: $$N = m(g-a)$$. In free fall: $$N = 0$$ (weightlessness).

nodes.label: Free Fall Weightlessness
nodes.note: When the elevator cable snaps ($$a = g$$ downward), the normal reaction vanishes: $$N = m(g-g) = 0$$. The passenger experiences apparent weightlessness.

nodes.label: Inertial Reference Frames
nodes.note: An inertial frame is one in which Newton's first law holds: an unforced particle maintains constant velocity. The ground frame is approximately inertial for JEE problems.

nodes.label: Constraints and Pulley Systems
nodes.note: String constraints, wedge contacts, Atwood machines, and spring dynamics with the sudden cut principle.

nodes.label: String Constraints
nodes.note: For an ideal massless inextensible string, the virtual work shortcut gives $$\sum \vec{T}_i \cdot \vec{a}_i = 0$$. This relates the accelerations of connected masses.

nodes.label: Movable Pulley
nodes.note: For a movable pulley with acceleration $$a_p$$ and connected masses with accelerations $$a_1$$ and $$a_2$$: $$a_p = \frac{a_1 + a_2}{2}$$.

nodes.label: Ideal String Assumptions
nodes.note: An ideal string is massless and inextensible. It cannot store energy, so the net work done by internal tension forces on the system is zero: $$\sum W_T = 0$$.

nodes.label: Wedge Contact Constraint
nodes.note: Two rigid bodies in contact cannot penetrate each other. The acceleration components perpendicular to the contact surface must match: $$a_{1,\perp} = a_{2,\perp}$$.

nodes.label: Atwood Machine
nodes.note: Two masses $$m_1 > m_2$$ connected by a light string over a frictionless pulley. The common acceleration is $$a = \frac{m_1 - m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$$ and tension is $$T = \frac{2m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$$.

nodes.label: Clamp Thrust
nodes.note: The thrust on the supporting pulley clamp is $$F_{\text{clamp}} = 2T = \frac{4m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}g$$. This is strictly less than the total weight $$(m_1 + m_2)g$$.

nodes.label: Spring Dynamics
nodes.note: Hooke's law gives the restoring force $$\vec{F}_s = -k\vec{x}$$. The product $$k \cdot L$$ is constant for a given spring, so cutting changes stiffness.

nodes.label: Sudden Cut Principle
nodes.note: When a string is cut, tension drops instantaneously: $$T(0^+) = 0$$. A spring force cannot change instantaneously: $$F_s(0^+) = F_s(0^-)$$.

nodes.label: Series and Parallel Springs
nodes.note: Series: $$\frac{1}{k_{\text{eq}}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}$$. Parallel: $$k_{\text{eq}} = k_1 + k_2$$.

nodes.label: Virtual Work Method
nodes.note: Since ideal strings cannot store energy, the net work done by internal tensions is zero: $$\sum \vec{T}_i \cdot \vec{v}_i = 0$$. This gives constraint relations between accelerations.

nodes.label: Friction Mechanics
nodes.note: Static and kinetic friction laws, angle of friction, angle of repose, and optimal pulling force.

nodes.label: Static Friction
nodes.note: Static friction is self-adjusting: $$0 \le f_s \le f_{s,\max} = \mu_s N$$. It matches the applied tangential force up to the limiting value.

nodes.label: Kinetic Friction
nodes.note: Once sliding begins, $$f_k = \mu_k N$$ where $$\mu_k \le \mu_s$$. Kinetic friction is nearly independent of sliding speed and contact area.

nodes.label: Direction of Kinetic Friction
nodes.note: Kinetic friction opposes the relative motion between the two contacted surfaces, not the absolute motion. On a two-block system, friction on the top block can act forward.

nodes.label: Angle of Friction
nodes.note: The angle of friction is $$\lambda = \tan^{-1}\mu_s$$. The total contact force is $$R = \sqrt{N^2 + f^2}$$ and ranges from $$N$$ to $$N\sqrt{1 + \mu_s^2}$$.

nodes.label: Total Contact Force
nodes.note: The resultant contact force $$\vec{R} = \vec{N} + \vec{f}$$ makes angle $$\lambda$$ with the normal when friction is at its limiting value: $$\tan\lambda = \frac{f_{s,\max}}{N} = \mu_s$$.

nodes.label: Angle of Repose
nodes.note: The maximum incline angle for static equilibrium is $$\theta_r = \tan^{-1}\mu_s = \lambda$$. At this angle, $$mg\sin\theta_r = \mu_s mg\cos\theta_r$$.

nodes.label: Acceleration Down Incline
nodes.note: For $$\theta > \theta_r$$, the body accelerates down: $$a = g(\sin\theta - \mu_k\cos\theta)$$. For $$\theta < \theta_r$$, static friction holds it at rest.

nodes.label: Minimum Pulling Force
nodes.note: To pull a block on a rough horizontal surface with force $$F$$ at angle $$\theta$$: $$F = \frac{\mu mg}{\cos\theta + \mu\sin\theta}$$. The minimum occurs at $$\theta = \lambda$$.

nodes.label: Minimum Pull Value
nodes.note: The minimum pulling force is $$F_{\min} = \frac{\mu mg}{\sqrt{1 + \mu^2}} = mg\sin\lambda$$, achieved when the pull angle equals the angle of friction.

nodes.label: Nature of Friction
nodes.note: Friction is an electromagnetic contact force that opposes relative sliding or the tendency of relative sliding. It is independent of apparent contact area.

nodes.label: Two-Block Friction Systems
nodes.note: Friction between two blocks with external force applied to either the top or bottom block. The slipping threshold depends on which block is pulled.

nodes.label: Force on Top Block
nodes.note: When force $$F$$ is applied to the top block $$m_1$$ on bottom block $$m_2$$ (smooth floor), the maximum acceleration of $$m_2$$ without slipping is $$a_{B,\max} = \frac{\mu m_1 g}{m_2}$$.

nodes.label: Top Pull Threshold
nodes.note: The threshold force for slipping is $$F_{\text{th}} = \mu m_1 g\left(1 + \frac{m_1}{m_2}\right)$$. Below this, both blocks move together at $$a = \frac{F}{m_1 + m_2}$$.

nodes.label: Force on Bottom Block
nodes.note: When force $$F$$ is applied to the bottom block $$m_2$$, the top block $$m_1$$ is accelerated only by friction. The maximum acceleration of $$m_1$$ without slipping is $$a_{A,\max} = \mu g$$.

nodes.label: Bottom Pull Threshold
nodes.note: The threshold force for slipping is $$F_{\text{th}} = \mu(m_1 + m_2)g$$. Below this, both blocks move together; above this, $$m_1$$ slides at constant $$a = \mu g$$.

nodes.label: Slipping Regimes
nodes.note: Below threshold, both blocks move with common acceleration. Above threshold, the pulled block accelerates independently while the other moves at constant friction-limited acceleration.

nodes.label: Friction as Accelerator
nodes.note: In the bottom-pull case, friction on the top block acts forward, accelerating it in the direction of motion. Friction is not always a retarding force.

nodes.label: Maximum Friction Force
nodes.note: The maximum friction force available between two blocks is $$f_{\max} = \mu m_1 g$$ where $$m_1$$ is the top block. This limits the acceleration that friction can transmit.

nodes.label: Photoelectric and Modern Physics
nodes.note: Modern physics began with the failure of classical waves to explain the photoelectric effect. Einstein's photon picture, $$K_{max} = h\nu - \phi$$, opened quantum theory.

nodes.label: Photoelectric Effect
nodes.note: Light ejects electrons only if each photon carries enough energy. The threshold condition is $$h\nu_0 = \phi$$, where $\phi$ is the work function.

nodes.label: Planck Photon Hypothesis
nodes.note: Light energy is quantized in packets: $$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda}$$, with $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J}\cdot\text{s}$. Higher frequency means more energetic photons, not brighter light.

nodes.label: Photon Energy Example
nodes.note: For $\lambda = 500\ \text{nm}$: $$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \approx 3.98 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J} \approx 2.48\ \text{eV}$$.

nodes.label: Einstein Photoelectric Equation
nodes.note: $$K_{max} = h\nu - \phi$$ converts photon energy into electron kinetic energy minus escape cost. It explains threshold frequency and instantaneous emission.

nodes.label: Einstein Equation Example
nodes.note: Light of $\lambda = 400\ \text{nm}$ hits a metal with $\phi = 2.0\ \text{eV}$: photon energy $E \approx 3.1\ \text{eV}$, so $K_{max} \approx 1.1\ \text{eV}$.

nodes.label: Stopping Potential
nodes.note: The reverse voltage that just stops the fastest electrons measures $K_{max}$: $$eV_s = h\nu - \phi$$. A plot of $V_s$ vs $\nu$ is linear with slope $h/e$.

nodes.label: Threshold Frequency and Work Function
nodes.note: Emission starts only above $$\nu_0 = \frac{\phi}{h}$$. Different metals have different $\phi$, so their thresholds differ.

nodes.label: Saturation Current vs Intensity
nodes.note: Saturation photocurrent is proportional to incident intensity (photon flux), while stopping potential is intensity-independent: $$i_{sat} \propto I, \ V_s \text{ independent of } I$$. More photons means more electrons, not faster electrons.

nodes.label: Radiation Pressure
nodes.note: For absorption, pressure is $$P = \frac{I}{c}$$; for perfect reflection, $$P = \frac{2I}{c}$$. Momentum transfer per photon is $p = E/c$.

nodes.label: Classical Wave Theory Failures
nodes.note: Wave theory predicts emission for any frequency given enough intensity and a time lag, both contradicted experimentally. Photons fix this via $$K_{max} = h\nu - \phi$$, independent of intensity.

nodes.label: Photocell I-V Curves
nodes.note: In a vacuum photocell, current rises with collector voltage then saturates: $$i_{sat} = \frac{ne}{t}$$. The stopping voltage intercept gives $h/e$.

nodes.label: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: De Broglie extended wave-particle duality to matter: $$\lambda = \frac{h}{p}$$.

nodes.label: De Broglie Wavelength
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: Every moving particle has an associated wavelength: $$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$. Macroscopic momenta give negligibly small $\lambda$, hiding wave behavior.

nodes.label: Electron Wavelength
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: An electron at $10^6\ \text{m}/\text{s}$ has $$\lambda = \frac{h}{mv} \approx 0.73\ \text{nm}$$, comparable to atomic spacings, hence diffraction.

nodes.label: Electron Accelerated Through V
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: After acceleration through potential $V$, $$\lambda = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2meV}} \approx \frac{1.227}{\sqrt{V}}\ \text{nm}$$. This sets the resolving scale of electron microscopes.

nodes.label: Davisson-Germer Experiment
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: Electrons scattered off nickel showed diffraction peaks at angles matching Bragg's law: $$2d\sin\theta = n\lambda$$. It confirmed matter waves directly.

nodes.label: Matter Waves in Bohr Orbits
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: Allowed orbits fit an integer number of de Broglie wavelengths: $$2\pi r_n = n\lambda = \frac{nh}{mv}$$. This recovers Bohr's angular momentum quantization.

nodes.label: Standing Wave Check
nodes.group: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
nodes.note: For the $n=2$ orbit of hydrogen, the circumference fits exactly two de Broglie wavelengths: $$2\pi r_2 = 2\lambda, \ \lambda = \frac{h}{mv}$$.

nodes.label: Atomic Structure
nodes.note: Rutherford's scattering established the nuclear atom. Bohr quantized its stationary states: $$mvr = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$$.

nodes.label: Rutherford Scattering
nodes.note: Alpha particles deflect off a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. Distance of closest approach is $$r_{min} = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0}\frac{2Ze^2}{K}$$.

nodes.label: Bohr Radius and Orbit Scaling
nodes.note: $$r_n = \frac{n^2}{Z}a_0, \ a_0 = 0.529\ \text{nm}$$. Radii grow as $n^2$, so outer orbits are much larger.

nodes.label: Bohr Energy Levels
nodes.note: $$E_n = -\frac{13.6\,Z^2}{n^2}\ \text{eV}$$. The negative sign means the electron is bound; ionization is the transition to $E = 0$.

nodes.label: Rydberg Formula and Spectral Series
nodes.note: $$\frac{1}{\lambda} = RZ^2\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2} - \frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$$. Lyman ends at $n=1$ (UV), Balmer at $n=2$ (visible), Paschen at $n=3$ (IR).

nodes.label: Balmer H-alpha
nodes.note: The H-alpha line is $n=3 \to n=2$: $$\frac{1}{\lambda} = R\left(\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{5R}{36}, \ \lambda \approx 656\ \text{nm}$$.

nodes.label: Ionization Energy and Excitation
nodes.note: Energy to remove an electron from level $n$ is $$E_{ion} = \frac{13.6\,Z^2}{n^2}\ \text{eV}$$. Excitation energy to the next level is the difference of level energies.

nodes.label: Quantum Mechanics
nodes.note: Quantum mechanics replaces trajectories with wavefunctions. The Schrodinger equation $$-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2\psi + V\psi = E\psi$$ governs it.

nodes.label: Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle
nodes.note: Position and momentum cannot both be sharp: $$\Delta x\,\Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2}$$. It forbids definite electron orbits inside the atom.

nodes.label: Uncertainty Estimate
nodes.note: If an electron is confined to a nucleus of size $\Delta x \approx 10^{-14}\ \text{m}$, then $$\Delta p \ge \frac{\hbar}{2\Delta x} \approx 5.3 \times 10^{-21}\ \text{kg m/s}$$, implying kinetic energies of tens of MeV.

nodes.label: Born Probability Interpretation
nodes.note: $$|\psi|^2$$ is the probability density: $$P(x) = |\psi(x)|^2$$. The wavefunction itself is not directly observable.

nodes.label: Four Quantum Numbers
nodes.note: $n$ sets shell, $l$ sets subshell shape ($0 \le l \le n-1$), $m_l$ sets orientation ($-l \le m_l \le l$), and $m_s = \pm\frac{1}{2}$ sets spin.

nodes.label: Electronic Configuration Rules
nodes.note: Aufbau fills lowest energy first with the $(n+l)$ rule, Pauli allows at most two electrons per orbital, and Hund maximizes spin multiplicity: $$S = \frac{1}{2}\times(\text{unpaired electrons})$$.

nodes.label: Nitrogen Example
nodes.note: Nitrogen ($Z = 7$): $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$. Hund puts all three $2p$ electrons in separate orbitals with parallel spins, giving $S = 3/2$.

nodes.label: X-Rays and Nuclear Physics
nodes.note: X-rays probe inner-shell transitions, radioactive decay is statistical, and mass defects power nuclei: $$\Delta E = \Delta m\,c^2$$.

nodes.label: Moseley's Law
nodes.note: Characteristic X-ray frequency follows $$\sqrt{\nu} = a(Z - b)$$. It reorganized the periodic table by atomic number.

nodes.label: Duane-Hunt Cutoff
nodes.note: The shortest bremsstrahlung wavelength from an X-ray tube is $$\lambda_{min} = \frac{hc}{eV}$$. Higher tube voltage shifts the cutoff to shorter wavelengths.

nodes.label: Radioactive Decay Law
nodes.note: $$N = N_0 e^{-\lambda t}, \ T_{1/2} = \frac{\ln 2}{\lambda}$$. Activity is $A = \lambda N$.

nodes.label: Binding Energy
nodes.note: $$B = \left[Zm_p + (A-Z)m_n - M\right]c^2$$. Peak binding energy per nucleon near iron explains fusion and fission energy release.

nodes.label: Compton Scattering
nodes.note: X-rays scattered off electrons show a wavelength shift: $$\Delta\lambda = \frac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$$. It proved photon momentum $p = h/\lambda$.

nodes.label: Half-Life Example
nodes.note: A sample with $T_{1/2} = 3$ days drops to $$\frac{N}{N_0} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{t/3}$$. After 9 days only $1/8$ remains.

nodes.label: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
nodes.note: Ray optics treats light as straight rays that reflect, refract, and bend through apertures, so geometry replaces wave analysis. Every JEE problem here is one sign convention plus one formula such as $$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$.

nodes.label: Reflection at Plane Surfaces
nodes.note: A plane mirror preserves object size and distance while flipping the perpendicular coordinate. The angle relation is always $$i = r$$.

nodes.label: Laws of Reflection
nodes.note: Incident ray, reflected ray, and normal are coplanar with $$i = r$$. In vector form the reflected direction is $$\hat{r} = \hat{i} - 2(\hat{i} \cdot \hat{n})\hat{n}$$.

nodes.label: Image Formation by a Plane Mirror
nodes.note: The image is virtual, erect, laterally inverted, and the same size as the object. Its distance behind the mirror equals the object distance: $$d_{image} = d_{object}$$.

nodes.label: Multiple Images Between Inclined Mirrors
nodes.note: Two mirrors at angle $$\theta$$ produce a finite ring of images when 360 degrees is an exact multiple of $$\theta$$. For symmetric object placement the count is $$n = \frac{360^\circ}{\theta} - 1$$.

nodes.label: Image Velocity in a Plane Mirror
nodes.note: Velocity components parallel to the mirror are unchanged, while the perpendicular component flips and adds the mirror's own motion. The rule is $$v_{I,\perp} = -v_{O,\perp} + 2v_{M,\perp}$$, with $$v_{I,\parallel} = v_{O,\parallel}$$.

nodes.label: Minimum Mirror for Full View
nodes.note: To see the full body, the ray must bend from head to foot through the mirror edge, so half the person's height suffices. The result is $$h_{min} = \frac{H}{2}$$ regardless of distance from the mirror.

nodes.label: Spherical Mirrors
nodes.note: Concave and convex mirrors focus rays using a spherical reflecting surface, and all their formulas flow from the paraxial approximation. The focal length is set purely by curvature: $$f = \frac{R}{2}$$.

nodes.label: Sign Convention and Focal Length
nodes.note: In the Cartesian convention, distances are measured from the pole with light travelling in the positive direction, so a concave mirror has $$f = -\frac{R}{2}$$ and a convex mirror has $$f = +\frac{R}{2}$$.

nodes.label: Mirror Formula and Lateral Magnification
nodes.note: Object, image, and focal distances are locked together for paraxial rays: $$\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{2}{R}$$. Lateral magnification follows as $$m = -\frac{v}{u}$$.

nodes.label: Longitudinal and Areal Magnification
nodes.note: Along the axis the magnification is the square of the transverse value, while areas scale by the square: $$m_L = -m^2$$ and $$m_A = m^2$$. The minus sign in $$m_L$$ signals the axial compression direction.

nodes.label: Newton's Formula for Conjugate Foci
nodes.note: Newton measures object and image distances from the focal points instead of the pole. The invariant is $$x_1 x_2 = f^2$$, with magnification $$m = -\frac{f}{x_1} = -\frac{x_2}{f}$$.

nodes.label: Image Velocity in Spherical Mirrors
nodes.note: Differentiating the mirror formula while the object moves gives an axial image speed scaled by the square of magnification. The result is $$\vec{v}_{I,\parallel} = -m^2 \vec{v}_{O,\parallel}$$ for motion along the principal axis.

nodes.label: Spherical Aberration
nodes.note: Marginal rays strike far from the pole and meet the axis closer than the paraxial focus, so a spherical mirror has no single sharp focus. The marginal focal length is $$f_{marg} = R - \frac{R}{2\cos\theta}$$, always shorter than $$R/2$$.

nodes.label: Refraction and Total Internal Reflection
nodes.note: A ray crossing a plane interface bends according to optical density and can be totally reflected when it starts in the denser medium. The governing relation is $$n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r$$.

nodes.label: Snell's Law and Refractive Index
nodes.note: Refraction follows from the constancy of the tangential wave component across the interface: $$n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r$$. The index also measures speed and wavelength change, $$n = \frac{c}{v} = \frac{\lambda_{air}}{\lambda_{med}}$$.

nodes.label: Apparent Depth and Normal Shift
nodes.note: Viewed normally from air, an object at depth $$t$$ in a medium of index $$\mu$$ appears closer: $$d_{app} = \frac{t}{\mu}$$. The upward normal shift is therefore $$\Delta t = t\left(1 - \frac{1}{\mu}\right)$$.

nodes.label: Lateral Displacement Through a Glass Slab
nodes.note: Two parallel refractions leave the emergent ray parallel to the incident one but offset sideways. The offset for slab thickness $$t$$ is $$s = \frac{t \sin(i - r)}{\cos r}$$.

nodes.label: Total Internal Reflection and Critical Angle
nodes.note: Beyond the critical angle the refracted ray vanishes and all energy returns to the denser medium. For a medium of index $$\mu$$ in air the critical angle obeys $$\sin i_c = \frac{1}{\mu}$$.

nodes.label: Optical Fibre and Acceptance Angle
nodes.note: A fibre traps light by repeated total internal reflection at the core-cladding boundary. The acceptance cone is fixed by the numerical aperture $$\text{NA} = \sin\theta_a = \sqrt{n_{core}^2 - n_{clad}^2}$$.

nodes.label: Apparent Motion Seen Through Refraction
nodes.note: An object seen through a plane interface is displaced toward the surface, since apparent depth is only $$t/\mu$$. Its apparent vertical speed therefore scales the same way: $$v_{app} = \frac{v}{\mu}$$.

nodes.label: Prisms and Dispersion
nodes.note: A prism bends light twice between non-parallel faces and separates colours because index varies with wavelength. Angle bookkeeping is $$A = r_1 + r_2$$ and $$\delta = i_1 + i_2 - A$$.

nodes.label: Prism Geometry and Deviation
nodes.note: Inside the prism the two refraction angles sum to the prism angle, giving the master relation $$A = r_1 + r_2$$. Total deviation is the entry and exit bends minus the wedge: $$\delta = i_1 + i_2 - A$$.

nodes.label: Minimum Deviation and Refractive Index
nodes.note: The deviation curve bottoms out where the ray passes symmetrically, so $$i_1 = i_2$$ and $$r_1 = r_2 = A/2$$. The prism formula then reads $$n = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{A + \delta_m}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$$.

nodes.label: Thin Prism Approximation
nodes.note: For a wedge of small apex angle all sines linearise, making deviation independent of the incident angle. The thin prism rule is $$\delta = (n - 1)A$$.

nodes.label: Condition of No Emergence
nodes.note: If the ray strikes the second face steeper than the critical angle it is totally internally reflected and never leaves. The limit is $$r_2 = 90^\circ$$, that is $$\sin r_2 = \frac{1}{n}$$ with $$r_2 = A - r_1$$.

nodes.label: Dispersion and Dispersive Power
nodes.note: Violet bends more than red because $$n_v > n_r$$, and the spread is measured by dispersive power. It depends only on the material: $$\omega = \frac{n_v - n_r}{n_y - 1} = \frac{\delta_v - \delta_r}{\delta_y}$$.

nodes.label: Achromatic and Direct-Vision Combinations
nodes.note: Two prisms can cancel either dispersion or net deviation but not both at once. Achromatism needs $$\omega_1 \delta_1 + \omega_2 \delta_2 = 0$$, while direct vision needs $$\delta_1 + \delta_2 = 0$$.

nodes.label: Lenses and Curved Refraction
nodes.note: Thin lenses refract twice at spherical surfaces and are fully described by their focal length and power. The working equation is $$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$.

nodes.label: Refraction at a Single Spherical Surface
nodes.note: A single curved interface relates object and image positions through the two indices and the radius of curvature. The formula is $$\frac{n_2}{v} - \frac{n_1}{u} = \frac{n_2 - n_1}{R}$$, and chaining two of them gives the thin lens equation.

nodes.label: Lens Maker's Formula
nodes.note: Two successive spherical refractions give the focal length from curvature and material alone: $$\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2}\right)$$. Immersing the lens in another medium replaces $$\mu - 1$$ by $$\frac{\mu}{\mu_{med}} - 1$$.

nodes.label: Thin Lens Formula and Magnification
nodes.note: Signs invert relative to mirrors because light passes through, giving $$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$. Transverse magnification is $$m = \frac{v}{u}$$, so a positive $$m$$ means erect.

nodes.label: Optical Power of Lenses
nodes.note: Power measures bending strength in dioptres when the focal length is in metres. It is $$P = \frac{1}{f_{(m)}}$$, and touching lenses add powers: $$P_{eq} = P_1 + P_2$$.

nodes.label: Image Velocity in Thin Lenses
nodes.note: Differentiating the lens formula with the object moving along the axis gives the same square law as mirrors. Axially the image moves as $$\vec{v}_{I,\parallel} = -m^2 \vec{v}_{O,\parallel}$$, so it outruns the object when $$|m| > 1$$.

nodes.label: Displacement or Conjugate Method
nodes.note: Sliding a lens between two positions that give the same sharp image on a fixed screen brackets the foci. Focal length follows from screen separation $$D$$ and lens travel $$d$$ as $$f = \frac{D^2 - d^2}{4D}$$, with $$m_1 m_2 = 1$$.

nodes.label: Cutting Thin Lenses
nodes.note: An equiconvex lens cut perpendicular to its axis becomes two plano-convex halves that are each weaker: $$f' = 2f$$. Cutting it along the axis instead leaves $$f' = f$$ but halves the aperture and the image intensity.

nodes.label: Combination of Thin Lenses
nodes.note: Lenses in contact simply add powers, while a gap $$d$$ between them subtracts a correction. The general result is $$\frac{1}{F} = \frac{1}{f_1} + \frac{1}{f_2} - \frac{d}{f_1 f_2}$$.

nodes.label: Silvering of Lenses
nodes.note: A silvered lens refracts, reflects, then refracts again, so the lens power counts twice alongside the mirror term. The equivalent power is $$P_{net} = \frac{2}{f} + \frac{2}{R}$$, and the device acts as a mirror of focal length $$F_{eq} = -\frac{1}{P_{net}}$$.

nodes.label: Optical Instruments
nodes.note: Instruments trade field of view for magnifying power by stacking lenses or by enlarging aperture. Angular magnification always compares $$M = \frac{\beta}{\alpha}$$ with the unaided eye at distance $$D$$.

nodes.label: Human Eye and Vision Defects
nodes.note: Myopia focuses light in front of the retina and is corrected by a diverging lens with $$f = -d_{far}$$. Hypermetropia needs a converging lens with $$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{D} - \frac{1}{d_{near}}$$.

nodes.label: Simple Microscope
nodes.note: A magnifier forms a virtual image at the near point for maximum magnification, or at infinity for a relaxed eye. Its power is $$M = 1 + \frac{D}{f}$$ at near point and $$M = \frac{D}{f}$$ for normal adjustment.

nodes.label: Compound Microscope
nodes.note: A short-focus objective builds a real intermediate image that the eyepiece magnifies. Near-point magnification is $$M = -\frac{v_o}{u_o}\left(1 + \frac{D}{f_e}\right)$$, with tube length $$L = v_o + f_e$$ at normal adjustment.

nodes.label: Astronomical Refracting Telescope
nodes.note: A large objective collects light from infinity and the eyepiece views its real image. At normal adjustment $$M = -\frac{f_o}{f_e}$$ and the tube length is $$L = f_o + f_e$$.

nodes.label: Resolving Power of Instruments
nodes.note: Diffraction limits how close two point sources can be and still be separated, as Rayleigh's criterion requires the peak to sit on the first minimum. A telescope resolves angles $$d\theta = \frac{1.22\lambda}{D}$$, and a microscope resolves distances $$d_{min} = \frac{1.22\lambda}{2\mu \sin\theta}$$.

nodes.label: Rotational Motion
nodes.note: Rigid body dynamics: inertia, torque, angular momentum, and rolling. Translate every idea from linear mechanics by mapping m to I, F to tau, and v to omega.

nodes.label: Rigid Body Kinematics
nodes.note: Definition of a rigid body, invariance of angular velocity, and the rotational kinematic equations. Geometry of a rotating body, before any force discussion.

nodes.label: Rigid Body Definition
nodes.note: A rigid body keeps fixed inter-particle distances, so its motion is fully described by the translation of one point plus rotation about it. Every point shares the same angular velocity.

nodes.label: Invariance of Angular Velocity
nodes.note: At any instant every particle has the same $\omega$ about any fixed axis: $$\vec{v} = \vec{\omega} \times \vec{r}$$. Thus $\omega$ is a property of the body, not of the chosen point.

nodes.label: Rotational Kinematic Equations
nodes.note: Under constant angular acceleration the rotational analogues of the translational laws hold: $$\omega = \omega_0 + \alpha t,\quad \theta = \omega_0 t + \tfrac{1}{2}\alpha t^2,\quad \omega^2 = \omega_0^2 + 2\alpha\theta$$. Use them exactly like the linear equations.

nodes.label: Angular Displacement
nodes.note: Angle in radians ties arc length to radius: $$\theta = \frac{s}{r},\quad v = r\omega,\quad a_t = r\alpha$$. Every circular quantity is just the linear one divided by r.

nodes.label: Centripetal Acceleration
nodes.note: Even steady rotation needs inward acceleration: $$a_c = \omega^2 r = \frac{v^2}{r}$$. Total acceleration combines it with the tangential part: $$a = \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}$$.

nodes.label: Linear-Rotational Analogy
nodes.note: Every translational law has a rotational twin: $$s \leftrightarrow \theta,\ v \leftrightarrow \omega,\ m \leftrightarrow I,\ F \leftrightarrow \tau,\ p \leftrightarrow L$$. Translate a familiar result rather than memorising a new one.

nodes.label: Moment of Inertia
nodes.note: Rotational inertia about axes, radius of gyration, axis-shift theorems, and the standard values. The quantity that plays the role of mass in rotation.

nodes.label: Definition and Radius of Gyration
nodes.note: Rotational inertia is $$I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2 = \int r^2 dm$$, with radius of gyration $$k = \sqrt{I/M}$$. Mass far from the axis dominates I.

nodes.label: Parallel Axis Theorem
nodes.note: Shifting from the centre of mass to a parallel axis adds $Md^2$: $$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$$. The CM axis always carries the smallest I.

nodes.label: Perpendicular Axis Theorem
nodes.note: For a planar lamina, the out-of-plane moment equals the sum of the two in-plane moments: $$I_z = I_x + I_y$$. This quickly yields, for a disc, $$I_z = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2$$.

nodes.label: Standard Moments of Inertia
nodes.note: Memorise the hierarchy $$I_{ring} = MR^2,\quad I_{disc} = \tfrac{1}{2}MR^2,\quad I_{solid\ sphere} = \tfrac{2}{5}MR^2,\quad I_{rod} = \tfrac{1}{12}ML^2$$. Smaller $I/MR^2$ means the body rolls faster.

nodes.label: Cavity by Negative Mass
nodes.note: A body with a cavity is the superposition of the full body minus the removed part: $$I = I_{full} - I_{removed}$$. The cavity piece's own CM offset then uses the parallel-axis theorem.

nodes.label: Torque and Rotational Dynamics
nodes.note: Torque as the rotational force, the rotational second law, and rotational work-energy. Dynamics of a body when the line of action misses the centre.

nodes.label: Definition of Torque
nodes.note: Torque is the moment of force about a point: $$\vec{\tau} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F},\quad \tau = rF\sin\phi$$. Its lever arm is the perpendicular distance from the axis to the line of force.

nodes.label: Rotational Second Law
nodes.note: Net torque produces angular acceleration: $$\tau_{net} = I\alpha$$, with the constraint equations of the problem supplying $\alpha$. It is the direct analogue of $F = ma$.

nodes.label: Angular Impulse and Work
nodes.note: Impulse of torque changes angular momentum, and torque does work through angle: $$\int \tau\, dt = \Delta L,\quad W = \int \tau\, d\theta,\quad P = \tau\omega$$. These are the rotational analogues of impulse and work.

nodes.label: Rotational Kinetic Energy
nodes.note: A spinning body stores $$K = \tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2$$. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis this replaces $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$; compare energies of differently shaped wheels at equal $\omega$.

nodes.label: Couple
nodes.note: Two equal opposite parallel forces form a pure moment: $$\tau = F \times d$$, independent of the pivot chosen. A couple spins a body without translating its CM.

nodes.label: Unwinding Yo-Yo and Hanging Mass
nodes.note: For a hanging mass $m$ on a string wrapped around a disc, Newton plus $\tau = I\alpha$ give $$a = \frac{g}{1 + I/mR^2}$$. The disc's inertia slows the descent.

nodes.label: Angular Momentum
nodes.note: Definition, conservation, and classic applications like the cue-ball strike. Conserved whenever external torque vanishes, exactly like linear momentum.

nodes.label: Definition of L
nodes.note: Angular momentum about a point is $$\vec{L} = \vec{r} \times m\vec{v}$$, and for a rigid body $$L = I\omega$$. Its direction follows the right-hand rule about the pivot.

nodes.label: Conservation of L
nodes.note: With zero net external torque, angular momentum is conserved: $$\tau_{ext} = 0 \Rightarrow L = const,\quad I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2$$. A skater pulling in her arms spins faster because $I$ drops.

nodes.label: Direction and Precession Idea
nodes.note: Torque changes L along its own direction: $$\vec{\tau} = \frac{d\vec{L}}{dt}$$. A spinning top precesses because gravity torques its angular momentum sideways, not downward.

nodes.label: Cue Ball Strike Height
nodes.note: A horizontal cue strike produces immediate pure rolling when $$h = \frac{R}{2}\left(1 + \frac{k^2}{R^2}\right)$$ above the centre, i.e. $7R/10$ for a solid sphere. Below this height the ball skids forward; above it, it back-spins.

nodes.label: Rolling Motion
nodes.note: Combined translation and rotation, the rolling constraint, instantaneous centre, incline dynamics, and energy partitioning. The richest rigid-body topic in JEE.

nodes.label: Konig's Theorem for KE
nodes.note: Total kinetic energy splits into CM translation and rotation about the CM: $$K = \tfrac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}^2 + \tfrac{1}{2}I_{cm}\omega^2$$. Each part is computed independently, then added.

nodes.label: Pure Rolling Condition
nodes.note: Rolling without slipping locks translation to rotation: $$v_{cm} = \omega R,\quad a_{cm} = \alpha R$$. Static friction enforces it and does no net work on the contact point.

nodes.label: Instantaneous Centre of Rotation
nodes.note: The contact point is momentarily at rest and acts as the pivot: every point's speed is $v = \omega d$ where $d$ is its distance from the contact. The top of a rolling wheel moves at $2v_{cm}$.

nodes.label: Rolling Down an Incline
nodes.note: Combining $Mg\sin\theta - f = Ma$ with $fR = I\alpha$ gives $$a = \frac{g\sin\theta}{1 + I/MR^2}$$. The race down the incline ranks ring last and solid sphere first.

nodes.label: Great Incline Race
nodes.note: Acceleration depends only on shape factor $\beta = I/MR^2$: smaller $\beta$ wins. Solid sphere ($2/5$) beats disc ($1/2$), which beats ring ($1$), independent of mass and radius.

nodes.label: Speed at the Base
nodes.note: Energy conservation gives $$v = \sqrt{\frac{2gh}{1 + I/MR^2}}$$, and travel time follows from $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$. No slipping means static friction, so mechanical energy is conserved.

nodes.label: Toppling versus Sliding
nodes.note: When a block tips over instead of sliding, set by geometry against friction. Decides the angle at which a block on an incline first gives way.

nodes.label: Normal Reaction Migration
nodes.note: As the incline steepens, the normal shifts toward the downhill edge: $$x = \frac{h}{2}\tan\theta$$-style balance of torques. Toppling begins when the normal reaches the lower corner.

nodes.label: Toppling vs Sliding Criterion
nodes.note: Sliding starts at $$\tan\theta = \mu_s$$ while toppling starts at $$\tan\theta = \frac{b}{h}$$ (base over height). The smaller of $\mu_s$ and $b/h$ decides the failure mode.

nodes.label: High-Yield Traps
nodes.note: Frequent exam pitfalls in rotational mechanics, gathered as quick diagnostics. Read after every problem for a one-line self-check.

nodes.label: Axis Choice Trap
nodes.note: Always write $\tau = I\alpha$ about an axis fixed in direction; for moving axes add the $M a_{cm} \times r$ correction. Mixing axes between L and alpha silently breaks conservation arguments.

nodes.label: Moment of Inertia Axis Trap
nodes.note: $I$ is always about a specified axis; quoting a single value without its axis is meaningless. Shift with $$I = I_{cm} + Md^2$$ only between parallel axes through the same orientation.

nodes.label: Rolling Energy Trap
nodes.note: In pure rolling on a fixed surface, static friction does no work, yet friction is essential to enforce $v = \omega R$. Do not add a $f \cdot s$ dissipation term.

nodes.label: Simple Harmonic Motion
nodes.note: SHM is motion under a restoring acceleration proportional to displacement: $$a = -\omega^2 x$$. Its energy oscillates between kinetic and potential forms.

nodes.label: SHM Fundamentals
nodes.note: The defining condition is linear restoring force: $$F = -kx \Rightarrow a = -\frac{k}{m}x$$.

nodes.label: Defining Condition
nodes.note: Acceleration is always directed toward the mean position and proportional to displacement: $$a = -\omega^2 x$$. Any system satisfying this oscillates in SHM.

nodes.label: Differential Equation of SHM
nodes.note: $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} + \omega^2 x = 0$$ with solution $$x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$. The angular frequency is $\omega = \sqrt{k/m}$.

nodes.label: Displacement, Velocity, Acceleration
nodes.note: $$v = A\omega\cos(\omega t + \phi), \ a = -A\omega^2\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$. Maximum speed at mean position: $$v_{max} = A\omega$$; maximum acceleration at extremes: $$a_{max} = A\omega^2$$.

nodes.label: Kinematics Example
nodes.note: For $x = 2\sin(3t)$ cm: $A = 2\ \text{cm}$, $\omega = 3\ \text{rad/s}$, so $$v_{max} = A\omega = 6\ \text{cm/s}, \ a_{max} = A\omega^2 = 18\ \text{cm/s}^2$$.

nodes.label: Phase and Reference Circle
nodes.note: $$x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)$$ maps to projection of uniform circular motion of radius $A$ and angular speed $\omega$. Velocity leads displacement by $\pi/2$.

nodes.label: Time Period and Frequency
nodes.note: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}, \ f = \frac{1}{T}, \ \omega = 2\pi f$$. Period is independent of amplitude for ideal SHM.

nodes.label: Period Example
nodes.note: A $0.5\ \text{kg}$ mass on a $200\ \text{N/m}$ spring: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{0.5/200} \approx 0.31\ \text{s}$$.

nodes.label: Energy in SHM
nodes.note: Total mechanical energy is conserved and fixed by amplitude: $$E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2$$.

nodes.label: Kinetic Energy
nodes.note: $$K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(A^2 - x^2)$$. It is maximum at the mean position and zero at extremes.

nodes.label: KE at Half Amplitude
nodes.note: At $x = A/2$: $$K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2\left(A^2 - \frac{A^2}{4}\right) = \frac{3}{4}E$$. Three-quarters of the energy is kinetic there.

nodes.label: Potential Energy
nodes.note: $$U = \frac{1}{2}kx^2 = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2 x^2$$. Stored energy grows quadratically with displacement from equilibrium.

nodes.label: Point Where K Equals U
nodes.note: Setting $K = U$ gives $$x = \frac{A}{\sqrt{2}}$$. At this point half the energy is kinetic and half potential.

nodes.label: Double-Frequency Energy Oscillation
nodes.note: Both $K$ and $U$ vary as $\sin^2$ or $\cos^2$, so each pulsates at twice the SHM frequency: $$f_{energy} = 2f_{SHM}$$.

nodes.label: Time-Average vs Position-Average Energy
nodes.note: Time-averaged over a cycle, $$\langle K \rangle = \langle U \rangle = \frac{E}{2}$$. Position-averaged over the path from $-A$ to $A$ gives a different split, a classic trap.

nodes.label: Spring-Mass Systems
nodes.note: Spring networks reduce to one equivalent constant. For springs, $$k = \frac{F}{x}$$ and $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k_{eq}}}$$.

nodes.label: Springs in Series
nodes.note: $$\frac{1}{k_{eq}} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2}$$. Equivalent constant is smaller, so the period increases.

nodes.label: Series Example
nodes.note: Two $100\ \text{N/m}$ springs in series give $k_{eq} = 50\ \text{N/m}$. A $2\ \text{kg}$ mass then oscillates with $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{2/50} \approx 1.26\ \text{s}$$.

nodes.label: Springs in Parallel
nodes.note: $$k_{eq} = k_1 + k_2$$. Stiffness adds, shortening the period.

nodes.label: Spring Cutting Rule
nodes.note: Cutting a spring into $n$ equal parts makes each part $n$ times stiffer: $$k' = nk$$. Shorter springs stretch less for the same force.

nodes.label: Two-Body Oscillator and Reduced Mass
nodes.note: Two masses on a spring oscillate with $$\mu = \frac{m_1m_2}{m_1 + m_2}, \ T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{\mu}{k}}$$. This collapses the two-body problem to one effective body.

nodes.label: Vertical Spring-Mass SHM
nodes.note: Gravity only shifts the equilibrium by $$x_0 = \frac{mg}{k}$$. Oscillation about the new equilibrium obeys $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}$$, unchanged.

nodes.label: Pendulum Dynamics
nodes.note: A pendulum is SHM for small angles. The simple pendulum period is $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$.

nodes.label: Simple Pendulum
nodes.note: For small angular displacement, restoring torque gives $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$$. Period grows with length and shrinks with gravity.

nodes.label: Seconds Pendulum
nodes.note: A pendulum with $T = 2\ \text{s}$ needs $$L = \frac{gT^2}{4\pi^2} \approx 0.994\ \text{m}$$. It is the classic seconds pendulum.

nodes.label: Pendulum in Accelerating Frames
nodes.note: In a lift accelerating at $a$, use $g_{eff} = g \pm a$: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g_{eff}}}$$. Free fall ($a = g$) gives infinite period.

nodes.label: Physical (Compound) Pendulum
nodes.note: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{mgd}}$$, where $I$ is moment of inertia about the pivot and $d$ is pivot-to-COM distance. It generalizes the simple pendulum.

nodes.label: Torsional Pendulum
nodes.note: $$T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{I}{\kappa}}$$, with $\kappa$ the torsional constant of the wire. Used to measure moments of inertia.

nodes.label: Large-Angle Correction
