nodes.label: Bayes' Theorem
nodes.note: $$P(E_i \mid A) = \frac{P(E_i)P(A \mid E_i)}{\sum_j P(E_j)P(A \mid E_j)}$$. Use it to invert cause and effect, e.g. defect rates across two machines.

nodes.label: Random Variables and Expectation
nodes.note: From experiments to numeric outcomes.

nodes.label: Discrete Random Variable
nodes.note: A variable X mapping outcomes to numbers has a probability mass function $p(x) = P(X = x)$ with $\sum p(x) = 1$. Number of heads in 3 tosses is the standard RV.

nodes.label: Expectation (Mean)
nodes.note: $$E(X) = \sum_i x_i\, p(x_i)$$ is the long-run average. Linearity $E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b$ simplifies most JEE items.

nodes.label: Variance and Standard Deviation
nodes.note: $$\text{Var}(X) = E(X^2) - [E(X)]^2 = \sum (x_i - \mu)^2 p(x_i)$$. SD is the square root of variance, so variance questions often test the shortcut formula.

nodes.label: Example: Expected Winnings
nodes.note: A game pays Rs 100 with probability 0.1 and loses Rs 20 with 0.9: $E = 0.1(100) - 0.9(20) = -8$, so it is unfavourable on average.

nodes.label: Distribution Tables
nodes.note: A valid distribution lists all x_i with probabilities summing to 1. Unknown constants in such problems come from $\sum p(x_i) = 1$.

nodes.label: Binomial Distribution
nodes.note: Bernoulli trials counted over n repetitions.

nodes.label: Bernoulli and Binomial Trials
nodes.note: Each trial has success probability p and failure q = 1 - p, independent of others. n trials give the binomial setting.

nodes.label: Binomial Probability Mass Function
nodes.note: $$P(X = r) = {}^nC_r\, p^r q^{\,n-r}$$. The probability of exactly r successes in n trials drives every JEE binomial PYQ.

nodes.label: Mean and Variance of Binomial
nodes.note: $$E(X) = np, \quad \text{Var}(X) = npq$$. Maximum probability occurs at the integer part of $(n+1)p$.

nodes.label: At Least One Success
nodes.note: $$P(X \ge 1) = 1 - P(X = 0) = 1 - q^n$$. Use the complement instead of summing the binomial tail.

nodes.label: Example: Coin Tosses
nodes.note: Probability of exactly 3 heads in 5 tosses: ${}^5C_3 (1/2)^3 (1/2)^2 = \frac{10}{32} = \frac{5}{16}$.

nodes.label: Other Distributions
nodes.note: Poisson, geometric, and normal appear as named limits or models.

nodes.label: Poisson Distribution
nodes.note: $$P(X = r) = \frac{e^{-\lambda} \lambda^r}{r!}$$ models rare events with rate lambda. It arises as the $n \to \infty, p \to 0$ limit of binomial.

nodes.label: Normal Distribution
nodes.note: A continuous curve with mean mu and SD sigma; about 68% of data lies within one sigma. Standardizing with $z = (x - \mu)/\sigma$ converts lookups to the standard normal table.

nodes.label: Example: Standardisation
nodes.note: If marks are $N(60, 10^2)$, then $P(X \ge 80) = P(Z \ge 2) \approx 0.0228$ from the standard normal table.

nodes.label: Geometric Distribution
nodes.note: Number of trials until the first success: $$P(X = k) = (1-p)^{k-1} p$$. Its mean $1/p$ measures waiting time for the first success.

nodes.label: Statistics
nodes.note: Central tendency, dispersion, and correlation.

nodes.label: Mean, Median and Mode
nodes.note: Mean $\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum x_i$, median is the middle ordered value, mode the most frequent. Skewed JEE data questions often distinguish which one misleads.

nodes.label: Variance, SD and Range
nodes.note: $$\sigma^2 = \frac{1}{n} \sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2$$ and the computational form $\sigma^2 = \overline{x^2} - \bar{x}^2$. Coefficient of variation $CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100$ compares data sets.

nodes.label: Correlation
nodes.note: $$r = \frac{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}{\sqrt{\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 \sum (y_i - \bar{y})^2}}$$ lies in $[-1, 1]$: $r = 1$ perfect positive linear relation, $r = -1$ perfect negative, $r = 0$ no linear relation.

nodes.label: Weighted Mean
nodes.note: Combine group means with weights: $$\bar{x} = \frac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i}$$. JEE uses it for combined averages of two sections with different sizes.

nodes.label: Coefficient of Variation
nodes.note: $$CV = \frac{\sigma}{\bar{x}} \times 100$$ compares relative spread of two data sets. The set with higher CV is less consistent.

nodes.label: Regression Lines
nodes.note: Least-squares lines of y on x and x on y both pass through $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$: $$y - \bar{y} = r\frac{\sigma_y}{\sigma_x}(x - \bar{x})$$. The product of the two slopes is $r^2$.

nodes.label: Quadratic Equations and Polynomial Theory
nodes.note: Quadratics are the most reliable scoring area in JEE Main algebra: Vieta, discriminant, location of roots and common roots appear in nearly every shift. The same machinery extends to cubics and rational functions.

nodes.label: Polynomials and Identities
nodes.note: Degree, the fundamental theorem and the equation-versus-identity distinction. Skipping the degree check is the most common way to lose an easy question.

nodes.label: Degree and the Fundamental Theorem
nodes.note: $P(x) = a_{n}x^{n} + \dots + a_{1}x + a_{0}$ with $a_{n} \neq 0$ has exactly $n$ roots in $\mathbb{C}$, so $P(x) = a_{n}(x-\alpha_{1})(x-\alpha_{2})\cdots(x-\alpha_{n})$. Degree counts roots with multiplicity.

nodes.label: Equation vs Polynomial
nodes.note: $P(x) = 0$ is an equation with finitely many solutions, while $P(x) \equiv 0$ is an identity true for every $x$. If $a = 0$ in $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ the degree drops and the quadratic formula becomes illegal.

nodes.label: Identity Theorem
nodes.note: $P(x) \equiv 0$ holds iff every coefficient is zero, so a quadratic satisfied by three distinct values forces $a = 0$, $b = 0$ and $c = 0$. A degree $n$ identity needs only $n+1$ test values to be proven.

nodes.label: Example: Proving an Identity
nodes.note: $\frac{(x-b)(x-c)}{(a-b)(a-c)} + \frac{(x-c)(x-a)}{(b-c)(b-a)} + \frac{(x-a)(x-b)}{(c-a)(c-b)} = 1$ holds at $x = a$, $x = b$ and $x = c$, so by the identity theorem it holds for all real $x$.

nodes.label: Parameterised Leading Coefficient
nodes.note: For $(\lambda-2)x^{2} + 2\lambda x + (\lambda-1) = 0$ first split into $\lambda = 2$, which is linear with one root, and $\lambda \neq 2$, which is quadratic with $D \ge 0$. Testing the discriminant alone misses the linear case.

nodes.label: Roots and Coefficients
nodes.note: Vieta's relations turn questions about roots into arithmetic on coefficients, with no need to solve the equation.

nodes.label: The Quadratic Formula
nodes.note: Completing the square gives $\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^{2} = \frac{D}{4a^{2}}$, hence $x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{D}}{2a}$ with $D = b^{2}-4ac$. Everything else in the chapter is built on this line.

nodes.label: Sum and Product of Roots
nodes.note: $\alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta = \frac{c}{a}$. Any symmetric condition on the roots can be rewritten using only these two numbers.

nodes.label: Difference of Roots
nodes.note: $|\alpha - \beta| = \frac{\sqrt{D}}{|a|}$, coming from $(\alpha-\beta)^{2} = (\alpha+\beta)^{2} - 4\alpha\beta$. Use it whenever the distance between roots is asked.

nodes.label: Transformation of Equations
nodes.note: Roots $\alpha+k$ come from $x = y-k$, roots $k\alpha$ from $x = y/k$, and reciprocal roots from $x = 1/y$. Substitute backwards into the original equation.

nodes.label: Example: Reciprocal Roots
nodes.note: Replacing $x$ by $1/y$ in $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ and clearing denominators gives $cy^{2}+by+a=0$, whose roots are $\frac{1}{\alpha}$ and $\frac{1}{\beta}$. The coefficients simply reverse.

nodes.label: Sign Conditions on Roots
nodes.note: Roots of opposite signs require only $\frac{c}{a} < 0$, which already forces $D > 0$. Both roots positive need $D \ge 0$ together with $-\frac{b}{2a} > 0$ and $\frac{c}{a} > 0$.

nodes.label: Symmetric Functions and Newton's Sums
nodes.note: Rewriting power sums of roots in terms of $S = \alpha+\beta$ and $P = \alpha\beta$, and the recurrence that generates them.

nodes.label: Symmetric Functions of Roots
nodes.note: $\alpha^{2}+\beta^{2} = S^{2}-2P$, $\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{\beta} = \frac{S}{P}$ and $\frac{\alpha}{\beta}+\frac{\beta}{\alpha} = \frac{S^{2}-2P}{P}$. Symmetry is what allows expression purely in $S$ and $P$.

nodes.label: Higher Power Sums
nodes.note: $\alpha^{3}+\beta^{3} = S^{3}-3SP$ and $\alpha^{4}+\beta^{4} = (S^{2}-2P)^{2} - 2P^{2}$. Expand from $S$ and $P$ rather than computing the roots.

nodes.label: Newton's Sums
nodes.note: For $S_{n} = p\alpha^{n} + q\beta^{n}$ the recurrence $aS_{n} + bS_{n-1} + cS_{n-2} = 0$ holds for every integer $n$. It answers very high powers without ever finding $\alpha$ or $\beta$.

nodes.label: Example: Running the Recurrence
nodes.note: With $S_{n} = \alpha^{n}+\beta^{n}$ the recurrence reads $S_{n} = -\frac{b}{a}S_{n-1} - \frac{c}{a}S_{n-2}$, seeded by $S_{0} = 2$ and $S_{1} = -\frac{b}{a}$. Two seeds generate every later term.

nodes.label: Nature of Roots
nodes.note: What the discriminant and the coefficient field together say about the roots, including the pairing theorems and their traps.

nodes.label: Real Field Classification
nodes.note: $D > 0$ gives real distinct roots, $D = 0$ gives the repeated root $-\frac{b}{2a}$, and $D < 0$ gives the conjugate pair $p \pm iq$ with $p = -\frac{b}{2a}$. Geometrically it is two cuts, one touch, or no touch of the $x$-axis.

nodes.label: Rational and Surd Roots
nodes.note: For $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $D > 0$, a perfect square $D$ gives rational roots and a non-square $D$ gives the surd pair $p \pm \sqrt{q}$. Surds therefore never appear alone.

nodes.label: Integral Root Conditions
nodes.note: Integer roots need $a, b, c \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $a = 1$ or $a$ dividing both $b$ and $c$, plus $D$ a perfect square. All three conditions together, not just the last one.

nodes.label: Conjugate Pair Theorems
nodes.note: Real coefficients force complex roots in pairs $z, \bar z$, and rational coefficients force surd pairs $p+\sqrt{q}, p-\sqrt{q}$. The pairing fails the moment coefficients leave that field.

nodes.label: The Conjugate Root Trap
nodes.note: $x^{2} - (2+i)x + (1+i) = 0$ has roots $1$ and $1+i$, with no conjugate present, because the coefficients are complex. Always check the field before invoking conjugate pairing.

nodes.label: Graph of a Quadratic
nodes.note: The parabola, its vertex, sign chart and range. Nearly every inequality question is answered by reading this picture.

nodes.label: Vertex and Axis
nodes.note: Completing the square gives $y = a\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^{2} - \frac{D}{4a}$, so the vertex is $V\left(-\frac{b}{2a}, -\frac{D}{4a}\right)$ and the axis is $x = -\frac{b}{2a}$.

nodes.label: Sign Chart with Two Roots
nodes.note: For $a > 0$ and roots $\alpha < \beta$, the expression is negative inside $(\alpha, \beta)$ and positive outside it. Reverse every sign when $a < 0$.

nodes.label: Strict Positivity Invariant
nodes.note: $ax^{2}+bx+c > 0$ for every real $x$ iff $a > 0$ and $D < 0$; it is always negative iff $a < 0$ and $D < 0$. Two conditions, always both required.

nodes.label: Example: Always Positive
nodes.note: For $x^{2}+x+1$ we get $D = 1-4 = -3 < 0$ with $a = 1 > 0$, so the curve floats above the axis and $x^{2}+x+1 > 0$ for all real $x$. It never vanishes.

nodes.label: Range on a Restricted Domain
nodes.note: On $[x_{1}, x_{2}]$ compare the endpoint values with the vertex value $-\frac{D}{4a}$ if $x_{v} = -\frac{b}{2a}$ lies inside the interval. Otherwise the function is monotone there and endpoints suffice.

nodes.label: Intercepts
nodes.note: The $y$-intercept is $(0, c)$ and the $x$-intercepts are $\left(\frac{-b \pm \sqrt{D}}{2a}, 0\right)$. When $D < 0$ the parabola meets neither axis except at $c$.

nodes.label: Location of Roots
nodes.note: The canonical conditions for placing roots relative to a point or an interval. Each regime combines the discriminant, the vertex and one sign test.

nodes.label: Both Roots Beyond a Point k
nodes.note: $\alpha, \beta > k$ needs $D \ge 0$, $-\frac{b}{2a} > k$ and $af(k) > 0$; for $\alpha, \beta < k$ the middle condition flips to $-\frac{b}{2a} < k$. Three conditions intersected.

nodes.label: k Between the Roots
nodes.note: $\alpha < k < \beta$ is captured by the single condition $af(k) < 0$, which automatically forces $D > 0$. This is the shortest condition in the whole topic.

nodes.label: Both Roots Inside an Interval
nodes.note: Roots inside $(k_{1}, k_{2})$ need $D \ge 0$, $k_{1} < -\frac{b}{2a} < k_{2}$, $af(k_{1}) > 0$ and $af(k_{2}) > 0$. Real roots, the vertex and both endpoints are all constrained.

nodes.label: Exactly One Root in an Interval
nodes.note: Exactly one root in the open interval $(k_{1}, k_{2})$ is simply $f(k_{1}) \cdot f(k_{2}) < 0$, since the curve must cross zero between the endpoints. Handle endpoints that are roots separately.

nodes.label: Interval Between the Roots
nodes.note: $\alpha < k_{1} < k_{2} < \beta$ needs $af(k_{1}) < 0$ and $af(k_{2}) < 0$, and either one already implies $D > 0$. The interval then sits in the negative well of an upward parabola.

nodes.label: Common Roots
nodes.note: Two quadratics sharing roots, decided either by an eliminant or by proportionality of coefficients.

nodes.label: Both Roots Common
nodes.note: Both roots are shared iff the coefficient triples are proportional: $\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}} = \frac{b_{1}}{b_{2}} = \frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}$. The two equations then describe the same parabola scaled.

nodes.label: Subtraction Gives a Candidate
nodes.note: Subtracting $x^{2}+ax+b=0$ and $x^{2}+cx+d=0$ yields the candidate $x = \frac{d-b}{a-c}$, which must be substituted back. If $a = c$ and $b \neq d$ there is no common root at all.

nodes.label: Complex Common Root Trap
nodes.note: If the first equation has real coefficients and $D_{1} < 0$, a shared complex root forces the conjugate to be shared too, so both roots are common and $\frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}} = \frac{b_{1}}{b_{2}} = \frac{c_{1}}{c_{2}}$.

nodes.label: Range of Rational Functions
nodes.note: Finding the range of a ratio of quadratics by reversing the problem into a discriminant condition on the numerator.

nodes.label: Discriminant Inversion
nodes.note: Cross-multiplying $y = \frac{a_{1}x^{2}+b_{1}x+c_{1}}{a_{2}x^{2}+b_{2}x+c_{2}}$ gives $(ya_{2}-a_{1})x^{2} + (yb_{2}-b_{1})x + (yc_{2}-c_{1}) = 0$, and requiring $D_{x} \ge 0$ yields an inequality in $y$ for the range.

nodes.label: Boundary and Asymptote Check
nodes.note: The candidate $y = \frac{a_{1}}{a_{2}}$, where the coefficient of $x^{2}$ dies, must be tested separately by substituting back into the linear equation. It is the horizontal asymptote $\lim_{x \to \pm\infty} y$.

nodes.label: Removable Common Factor Trap
nodes.note: If $(x-k)$ cancels from numerator and denominator, the graph has a hole at $x = k$ and the value $\frac{k-\alpha}{k-\beta}$ is never attained. Delete it from the otherwise computed range.

nodes.label: Higher Degree Polynomials
nodes.note: Generalised Vieta, cubics, roots in progressions and sign counting. The same symmetric-function logic simply scales up.

nodes.label: Generalised Vieta Formulas
nodes.note: For degree $n$, $\sum \alpha_{i} = -\frac{a_{n-1}}{a_{n}}$, $\sum_{i<j}\alpha_{i}\alpha_{j} = \frac{a_{n-2}}{a_{n}}$ and $\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\cdots\alpha_{n} = (-1)^{n}\frac{a_{0}}{a_{n}}$. Signs alternate from the top.

nodes.label: Cubic Equations
nodes.note: For $ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d=0$ the roots obey $\alpha+\beta+\gamma = -\frac{b}{a}$, $\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha = \frac{c}{a}$ and $\alpha\beta\gamma = -\frac{d}{a}$.

nodes.label: Roots in AP, GP and HP
nodes.note: For roots in AP assume $t-d, t, t+d$, giving $t = -\frac{b}{3a}$; for GP use $\frac{t}{r}, t, tr$, giving $t^{3} = -\frac{d}{a}$; for HP substitute $x = \frac{1}{y}$ to get roots in AP.

nodes.label: Descartes' Rule of Signs
nodes.note: The number of positive real roots equals the sign changes among non-zero coefficients of $P(x)$, or is less by an even number; for negative roots apply the rule to $P(-x)$.

nodes.label: Turning Points
nodes.note: $P'(x) = 0$ locates the local extrema, so a degree $n$ polynomial has at most $n-1$ turning points. Between two distinct real roots there is always one turning point.

nodes.label: Reducible and Symmetric Equations
nodes.note: Higher-degree equations that collapse into a quadratic after a smart substitution.

nodes.label: Reciprocal (Palindromic) Equations
nodes.note: For $ax^{4}+bx^{3}+cx^{2}+bx+a=0$ divide by $x^{2}$ and set $u = x + \frac{1}{x}$, using $x^{2} + \frac{1}{x^{2}} = u^{2}-2$. The quartic becomes a quadratic in $u$.

nodes.label: The |u| >= 2 Condition
nodes.note: Solving $x + \frac{1}{x} = u$ gives real $x$ iff $|u| \ge 2$, and for $|u| < 2$ the roots are non-real conjugates. Reject the $u$ values that fail this test.

nodes.label: Equations with a Modulus
nodes.note: In $ax^{2}+b|x|+c=0$ substitute $u = |x| \ge 0$ and solve for $u$. Each $u > 0$ yields two roots $x = \pm u$, $u = 0$ yields one, and negative $u$ yields none.

nodes.label: Example: Counting Roots
nodes.note: For $x^{2} - 5|x| + 6 = 0$ the substitution gives $u = 2$ or $u = 3$, so there are four real roots $\pm 2$ and $\pm 3$. Count in $u$ first, then translate back to $x$.

nodes.label: Sequences, Series and Progressions
nodes.note: Sequences and series underpin JEE algebra: AP, GP, HP, arithmetico-geometric series, and telescoping methods. Expect one question every year built on nth-term and sum identities.

nodes.label: Sequence Fundamentals
nodes.note: Definitions and core invariants that link a sequence to its partial sums. These identities are the entry point for almost every JEE series problem.

nodes.label: Sequence as a Function
nodes.note: A sequence assigns each natural number n a unique term: $$a_n = f(n), \ n \in \mathbb{N}$$. Finite and infinite types both appear in sum-of-n problems.

nodes.label: Series and Partial Sums
nodes.note: A series is the indicated sum of terms, and its partial sum is $$S_n = \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k$$. JEE problems often hand you S_n and ask for the sum of specific terms.

nodes.label: Term from Sum Relation
nodes.note: Recover the nth term from the partial sums: $$a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \ (n \ge 2), \ a_1 = S_1$$. The n >= 2 restriction is a classic off-by-one trap.

nodes.label: Mini-Example: S_n Given
nodes.note: If $S_n = 2n^2 + 3n$, then $a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} = 4n + 1$ for $n \ge 2$, and $a_1 = S_1 = 5$, which matches $4(1)+1$.

nodes.label: Finite vs Infinite Sums
nodes.note: Finite series stop at a last term, while infinite series need a convergence check before any sum formula applies. $$S_\infty = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k$$ exists only when terms vanish fast enough.

nodes.label: Arithmetic Progression
nodes.note: The workhorse of JEE sequences: constant difference between consecutive terms. Most questions reduce to the nth-term or sum formula.

nodes.label: Common Difference
nodes.note: The difference is constant: $$d = a_{k+1} - a_k$$. A zero d gives a constant sequence, worth spotting in modified progressions.

nodes.label: nth Term of an AP
nodes.note: The general term is $$T_n = a + (n-1)d$$. Asking which term equals X is a direct linear equation in n.

nodes.label: Sum of n Terms of AP
nodes.note: The sum of the first n terms is $$S_n = \frac{n}{2}\left[2a + (n-1)d\right]$$. It is quadratic in n, so a quadratic S_n signals an AP.

nodes.label: Arithmetic Mean
nodes.note: The middle term of three terms in AP is their mean: $$b = \frac{a+c}{2}$$. Inserting k AMs between a and b is a standard JEE step.

nodes.label: Equidistant Term Property
nodes.note: Terms equidistant from the ends sum equally: $$a_k + a_{n+1-k} = a_1 + a_n$$. Use it to shortcut sums of symmetric selected terms.

nodes.label: Example: Sum of an AP
nodes.note: For $3, 7, 11, \dots$ ($a=3, d=4$): $S_{20} = \frac{20}{2}[6 + 19\cdot 4] = 820$. JEE wraps this in word problems about arithmetic totals.

nodes.label: Geometric Progression
nodes.note: Constant ratio between consecutive terms. Infinite GP sums and mean relations are heavily tested.

nodes.label: Common Ratio
nodes.note: Each term is a fixed multiple of the previous: $$r = \frac{a_{k+1}}{a_k}$$. The sign and magnitude of r decide monotonicity and convergence.

nodes.label: nth Term of a GP
nodes.note: The general term is $$T_n = ar^{n-1}$$. Logarithms convert GP problems into AP problems, a standard JEE manipulation.

nodes.label: Sum of n Terms of GP
nodes.note: For r not equal to 1 the partial sum is $$S_n = a\frac{r^n - 1}{r - 1}$$. The $r = 1$ case collapses to $S_n = na$.

nodes.label: Infinite Geometric Sum
nodes.note: When $|r| < 1$ the series converges: $$S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r}$$. This single formula powers recurring-decimal and geometric-tail questions.

nodes.label: Geometric Mean
nodes.note: For three terms in GP, the middle is the geometric mean: $$b^2 = ac$$. Two positive numbers have GM $\sqrt{ac}$, linking to the AM-GM-HM chain.

nodes.label: Harmonic Progression
nodes.note: Reciprocals form an AP. HP questions are usually disguised AM/GM problems.

nodes.label: HP Definition
nodes.note: A sequence is harmonic when its reciprocals form an AP: $$\frac{1}{a_{k+1}} - \frac{1}{a_k} = \text{constant}$$. Its nth term mirrors the AP structure on reciprocals.

nodes.label: nth Term of an HP
nodes.note: If reciprocals are an AP with first A and difference D, then $$T_n = \frac{1}{A + (n-1)D}$$. Take reciprocals first, then apply AP formulas.

nodes.label: Harmonic Mean
nodes.note: The harmonic mean of two numbers is $$H = \frac{2ab}{a+b}$$. HM of a and b is the reciprocal of the AM of $1/a$ and $1/b$.

nodes.label: Example: HM of Two Numbers
nodes.note: HM of 2 and 6 is $H = \frac{2 \cdot 2 \cdot 6}{2 + 6} = 3$, and $2, 3, 6$ are in HP since $\frac{1}{2}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{6}$ are in AP.

nodes.label: Means and Inequalities
nodes.note: AM-GM-HM relations and Cauchy-Schwarz give quick answers to max-min JEE questions.

nodes.label: AM-GM-HM Chain
nodes.note: For positive reals the three means are ordered: $$AM \ge GM \ge HM$$. Equality holds iff all numbers are equal.

nodes.label: Weighted AM-GM
nodes.note: Weights turn the inequality into $$w_1 a_1 + w_2 a_2 \ge a_1^{w_1} a_2^{w_2}, \ w_1 + w_2 = 1$$. Handy for optimization under a constraint.

nodes.label: Cauchy-Schwarz Inequality
nodes.note: $$(a_1^2 + a_2^2)(b_1^2 + b_2^2) \ge (a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2)^2$$ bounds a dot product by the product of norms. Common in sum-bound questions.

nodes.label: Example: Max Product
nodes.note: For $x + y = 10$, AM-GM gives $\sqrt{xy} \le 5$, so the product $xy \le 25$, maximized at $x = y = 5$.

nodes.label: Arithmetico-Geometric Progression
nodes.note: Product of an AP and a GP term by term. The shift-and-subtract derivation is the key skill.

nodes.label: AGP Term Structure
nodes.note: Each term multiplies an AP factor by a GP factor: $$T_n = [a + (n-1)d]\, r^{n-1}$$. Recognize the mixed structure before applying formulas.

nodes.label: AGP Finite Sum
nodes.note: Multiply $S_n$ by r and subtract to collapse the series: $$S_n = \frac{a - [a+(n-1)d]r^n}{1-r} + \frac{dr(1 - r^{n-1})}{(1-r)^2}$$. The shift-and-subtract idea is asked conceptually in JEE.

nodes.label: AGP Infinite Sum
nodes.note: For $|r| < 1$: $$S_\infty = \frac{a}{1-r} + \frac{dr}{(1-r)^2}$$. The second term is the correction from the arithmetic part.

nodes.label: Example: 2 + 8 + 24 + 64
nodes.note: For $S = 1\cdot 2 + 2\cdot 4 + 3\cdot 8 + \dots$ the AGP has $a=1, d=1, r=2$; since $|r|>1$ only finite partial sums exist, found via shift-and-subtract.

nodes.label: Summation Methods
nodes.note: Difference tables, telescoping, and sigma identities cover non-standard series in JEE.

nodes.label: Method of Differences
nodes.note: Successive differences reveal the polynomial degree of the nth term: $$\Delta T_n = T_{n+1} - T_n$$. If the first differences are constant, T_n is linear; two rounds give a quadratic.

nodes.label: Telescoping Series
nodes.note: Write each term as a difference and cancel in between: $$\sum_{k=1}^{n}(V_k - V_{k-1}) = V_n - V_0$$. Partial-fraction splits set this up.

nodes.label: Example: Telescoping Sum
nodes.note: $\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{1}{k(k+1)} = \sum \left(\frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k+1}\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{n+1}$, a classic telescoping collapse.

nodes.label: Standard Sigma Identities
nodes.note: $$\sum_{k=1}^n k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \quad \sum_{k=1}^n k^2 = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}, \quad \sum_{k=1}^n k^3 = \left[\frac{n(n+1)}{2}\right]^2$$. Memorize all three for direct use.

nodes.label: Sets and Relations
nodes.note: Sets, counting and relations form the language JEE uses to state algebra and probability problems. Expect one or two direct questions per shift, usually on Venn counting or on checking an equivalence relation.

nodes.label: Set Fundamentals
nodes.note: How a set is written and which standard number sets exist. Everything later depends on reading a set-builder rule correctly.

nodes.label: Definition and Notation
nodes.note: A set is a well-defined collection of distinct objects, and $a \in A$ states membership while $a \notin A$ denies it. JEE exploits 'well-defined' by offering vague collections such as 'the best cricketers in India'.

nodes.label: Standard Number Sets
nodes.note: The usual chain is $\mathbb{N} \subset \mathbb{W} \subset \mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R} \subset \mathbb{C}$. Rational numbers are $\mathbb{Q} = \{p/q : p, q \in \mathbb{Z}, \ q \neq 0\}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ covers every complex number.

nodes.label: Roster and Set-Builder Form
nodes.note: Roster form lists the elements, set-builder form gives the defining rule. Always expand the rule into a list before you start counting.

nodes.label: Example: Roster Expansion
nodes.note: The builder $\{x \in \mathbb{Z} : |x| \le 3\}$ expands to $\{-3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\}$, so the cardinality is $n(A) = 7$.

nodes.label: Types of Sets
nodes.note: Classification by size and by comparison. The empty set trap and the equal-versus-equivalent distinction are the two favourites of paper setters.

nodes.label: Empty and Singleton Sets
nodes.note: The empty set satisfies $n(\phi) = 0$, yet $\{\phi\}$ is a singleton with exactly one element. Options built on this confusion appear almost every year.

nodes.label: Finite, Infinite and Cardinality
nodes.note: The cardinality $n(A)$ counts distinct elements of a finite set, and $n(\phi) = 0$. Infinite sets such as $\mathbb{R}$ carry no finite count, so count questions always restrict to a finite universe.

nodes.label: Equal vs Equivalent Sets
nodes.note: Equivalent means $n(A) = n(B)$, while equal means $A \subseteq B$ and $B \subseteq A$ together, giving $A = B$. Equal sets are always equivalent, but equivalent sets need not be equal.

nodes.label: Subsets and Power Sets
nodes.note: Subset logic and the $2^n$ power-set count drive quick option-based questions where all subsets must be enumerated.

nodes.label: Subset and Proper Subset
nodes.note: $A \subseteq B$ means every element of $A$ lies in $B$, and $A \subset B$ adds $A \neq B$. The empty set is a subset of every set, which makes it the default element of any intersection.

nodes.label: Power Set
nodes.note: $P(A)$ collects all subsets of $A$, so $n(A) = n$ gives $n(P(A)) = 2^n$. The power set is never empty because $\phi \in P(A)$.

nodes.label: Example: Power Set of a Two-Element Set
nodes.note: For $A = \{1, 2\}$ we get $P(A) = \{\phi, \{1\}, \{2\}, \{1, 2\}\}$. Here $A \in P(A)$ is true but $\{A\} \notin P(A)$, a distinction worth memorising.

nodes.label: Disjoint and Comparable Sets
nodes.note: Two sets are disjoint when $A \cap B = \phi$, and comparable when one contains the other. Disjointness is exactly what lets you drop the intersection term in counting formulas.

nodes.label: Real Intervals
nodes.note: Closed and open intervals are subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, for example $[a, b] = \{x \in \mathbb{R} : a \le x \le b\}$. Mixed forms such as $[a, b)$ show up constantly in domain and range answers.

nodes.label: Set Operations and Algebraic Laws
nodes.note: Union, intersection, difference, symmetric difference and complement, together with the laws that regroup them. Every De Morgan question reduces to one of these rules.

nodes.label: Union of Sets
nodes.note: $A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$ gathers every element of either set. It is commutative and associative, with identity $A \cup \phi = A$.

nodes.label: Intersection of Sets
nodes.note: $A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}$ keeps only common elements, and $A \cap \phi = \phi$. Intersection distributes over union: $A \cap (B \cup C) = (A \cap B) \cup (A \cap C)$.

nodes.label: Difference of Sets
nodes.note: $A - B = A \cap B'$ removes from $A$ everything that also lies in $B$. Consequently $A - B = A$ holds exactly when $A \cap B = \phi$.

nodes.label: Symmetric Difference
nodes.note: $A \Delta B = (A - B) \cup (B - A)$ is the exclusive part of the union, and $n(A \Delta B) = n(A) + n(B) - 2n(A \cap B)$. It distributes over intersection: $A \cap (B \Delta C) = (A \cap B) \Delta (A \cap C)$.

nodes.label: Complement and De Morgan Laws
nodes.note: De Morgan gives $(A \cup B)' = A' \cap B'$ and $(A \cap B)' = A' \cup B'$, alongside $A \cup A' = U$ and $A \cap A' = \phi$. Flip the operation and swap the sets.

nodes.label: Example: Complement Counting
nodes.note: If $n(U) = 50$ and $n(A \cap B) = 12$, then $n((A \cap B)') = n(U) - n(A \cap B) = 38$. Complement questions are subtraction from the universe and nothing more.

nodes.label: Commutative, Associative and Idempotent Laws
nodes.note: $A \cup B = B \cup A$, $(A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)$ and $A \cup A = A$, with mirror laws for intersection. These let you regroup a long union while shading a Venn diagram.

nodes.label: Cardinality and Counting
nodes.note: Inclusion-exclusion on finite sets. This is where most JEE Main set questions actually live.

nodes.label: Two-Set Inclusion-Exclusion
nodes.note: $n(A \cup B) = n(A) + n(B) - n(A \cap B)$, and the intersection term disappears for disjoint sets. This is the most used counting identity in the chapter.

nodes.label: Example: Survey Counting
nodes.note: If 30 students like physics, 25 like chemistry and 10 like both, then $n(P \cup C) = 30 + 25 - 10 = 45$ of the surveyed students like at least one.

nodes.label: Three-Set Inclusion-Exclusion
nodes.note: $n(A \cup B \cup C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - n(A \cap B) - n(B \cap C) - n(C \cap A) + n(A \cap B \cap C)$. Add singles, subtract pairs, then add back the triple overlap.

nodes.label: Elements in Exactly Two Sets
nodes.note: $n(A \cap B) + n(B \cap C) + n(C \cap A) - 3n(A \cap B \cap C)$ counts elements lying in precisely two of the three sets. The coefficient 3 strips out the triple overlap counted in every pair.

nodes.label: Elements in Exactly One Set
nodes.note: $n(A) + n(B) + n(C) - 2[n(A \cap B) + n(B \cap C) + n(C \cap A)] + 3n(A \cap B \cap C)$ counts elements in exactly one set. Most-attempted region in a three-circle Venn diagram.

nodes.label: Counting Differences
nodes.note: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$ and $n(B - A) = n(B) - n(A \cap B)$. Use these when only one region is asked, instead of shading the whole diagram.

nodes.label: Cartesian Products
nodes.note: Ordered pairs and product sets. This is the bridge from sets to relations and functions, so it appears in both chapters.

nodes.label: Ordered Pairs
nodes.note: $(a_1, b_1) = (a_2, b_2)$ holds iff $a_1 = a_2$ and $b_1 = b_2$, so order matters and $(1, 2) \neq (2, 1)$. This single idea is why $(a, b) \neq (b, a)$ in counting questions.

nodes.label: Cartesian Product Definition
nodes.note: $A \times B = \{(a, b) : a \in A \text{ and } b \in B\}$ and $n(A \times B) = n(A) n(B)$. Also $A \times B = \phi$ exactly when at least one of the sets is empty.

nodes.label: Properties of the Product
nodes.note: $(A \times B) \cap (C \times D) = (A \cap C) \times (B \cap D)$, and $A \subseteq B, C \subseteq D$ implies $A \times C \subseteq B \times D$. Distribution over union, intersection and difference all hold.

nodes.label: Example: Shared Ordered Pairs
nodes.note: If $A$ and $B$ have $n$ elements in common, then $A \times B$ and $B \times A$ share exactly $n^2$ ordered pairs, because both coordinates must be shared.

nodes.label: Relations
nodes.note: A relation is simply a subset of a product set. Domain, range, inverse and composition follow from that reading.

nodes.label: Relation as a Subset
nodes.note: A relation $R$ from $A$ to $B$ is any subset of $A \times B$, written $aRb$ for $(a, b) \in R$. With $n(A) = m$ and $n(B) = n$ there are $2^{mn}$ possible relations.

nodes.label: Domain, Range and Codomain
nodes.note: $\text{Domain}(R) = \{a \in A : (a, b) \in R\}$ collects the first entries and the range collects the second. Passing to $R^{-1}$ swaps domain and range.

nodes.label: Reflexive, Symmetric and Transitive
nodes.note: Reflexive demands $(a, a) \in R$ for all $a$, symmetric demands $aRb \Rightarrow bRa$, and transitive demands $aRb, bRc \Rightarrow aRc$. One missing pair destroys each property.

nodes.label: Example: Counting Reflexive Relations
nodes.note: On an $n$-element set the diagonal pairs are forced, so reflexive relations number $2^{n^2 - n}$. For $n = 3$ that is $2^6 = 64$ out of $2^9 = 512$ total relations.

nodes.label: Inverse and Composition
nodes.note: $R^{-1} = \{(b, a) : (a, b) \in R\}$ and $(S \circ R)^{-1} = R^{-1} \circ S^{-1}$. Composition is not commutative in general, so the order of the arrows matters.

nodes.label: Equivalence Relations
nodes.note: Reflexive, symmetric and transitive at once. Such relations split the set into clean, non-overlapping classes.

nodes.label: Definition of an Equivalence Relation
nodes.note: A relation that is simultaneously reflexive, symmetric and transitive. Standard examples are equality, congruence modulo $n$ and 'born in the same year'.

nodes.label: Equivalence Classes
nodes.note: $[a] = \{x \in A : (x, a) \in R\}$, and any two classes are either identical or disjoint. The classes partition $A$, so their cardinalities add up to $n(A)$.

nodes.label: Example: Classes Modulo 3
nodes.note: Congruence mod 3 splits $\{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}$ into the three classes $\{-2, 1\}$, $\{-1, 2\}$ and $\{0, 3\}$, which are disjoint and together cover the set.

nodes.label: Combining Equivalence Relations
nodes.note: If $R$ and $S$ are equivalence relations then $R \cap S$ is again an equivalence relation, but $R \cup S$ need not be. The inverse $R^{-1}$ of an equivalence relation is always one.

nodes.label: Trigonometry
nodes.note: Ratios, allied angles, compound and multiple-angle formulas, triangle identities, equations, and height-distance applications. JEE tests formula recall under algebraic manipulation.

nodes.label: Trigonometric Ratios and Identities
nodes.note: Definitions and the fundamental identities that everything else uses.

nodes.label: Six Ratios
nodes.note: Sine, cosine, tangent and their reciprocals on a right triangle: $$\sin \theta = \frac{opp}{hyp}, \ \cos \theta = \frac{adj}{hyp}, \ \tan \theta = \frac{opp}{adj}$$. The reciprocal pairings $csc = 1/sin$, $sec = 1/cos$, $cot = 1/tan$ complete the set.

nodes.label: Reciprocal Relations
nodes.note: Cosecant, secant, and cotangent are reciprocals: $$\csc \theta = \frac{1}{\sin \theta}, \ \sec \theta = \frac{1}{\cos \theta}, \ \cot \theta = \frac{1}{\tan \theta}$$. JEE options often hide reciprocal traps among near-identical choices.

nodes.label: Pythagorean Identities
nodes.note: $$\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta = 1, \ 1 + \tan^2 \theta = \sec^2 \theta, \ 1 + \cot^2 \theta = \csc^2 \theta$$. Divide the first identity by $\cos^2$ or $\sin^2$ to get the other two.

nodes.label: Standard Exact Values
nodes.note: Key angles: $$\sin 30^\circ = \frac{1}{2}, \ \cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2}, \ \tan 45^\circ = 1$$. A memory table for $0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ, 90^\circ$ is non-negotiable.

nodes.label: Identity Reduction
nodes.note: Simplify compound expressions by rewriting in sine and cosine: e.g. $$\tan \theta + \cot \theta = \frac{\sin^2 \theta + \cos^2 \theta}{\sin \theta \cos \theta} = \frac{2}{\sin 2\theta}$$. JEE 'prove that' items demand this conversion.

nodes.label: Example: Simplification
nodes.note: $\frac{\sin \theta}{1 - \cos \theta} = \cot(\theta/2)$ follows by multiplying numerator and denominator by $1 + \cos \theta$ and using $1 - \cos^2 = \sin^2$.

nodes.label: Allied Angles and ASTC
nodes.note: Signs and reductions for angles in all quadrants.

nodes.label: ASTC Rule
nodes.note: Quadrant signs: all positive in I, sine positive in II, tangent positive in III, cosine positive in IV. 'All Snakes Take Coffee' is the memory hook for which ratios are positive in each quadrant.

nodes.label: Allied Angle Reduction
nodes.note: Reduce any angle to a first-quadrant reference: $$\sin(90^\circ \pm \theta) = \cos \theta, \ \sin(180^\circ \pm \theta) = \mp \sin \theta$$. Sign from ASTC, cofunction swap for odd multiples of 90.

nodes.label: Mini-Example: Reduction
nodes.note: $\cos 150^\circ = \cos(180^\circ - 30^\circ) = -\cos 30^\circ = -\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$. Minutes of error in sign sink most JEE one-markers.

nodes.label: Compound Angles
nodes.note: Sum and difference formulas plus product-to-sum conversions.

nodes.label: Addition and Subtraction
nodes.note: $$\sin(A \pm B) = \sin A \cos B \pm \cos A \sin B$$ $$\cos(A \pm B) = \cos A \cos B \mp \sin A \sin B$$ $$\tan(A \pm B) = \frac{\tan A \pm \tan B}{1 \mp \tan A \tan B}$$. Every compound-angle JEE item starts here.

nodes.label: Sum-to-Product (C and D) Formulas
nodes.note: $$\sin C + \sin D = 2 \sin \frac{C+D}{2} \cos \frac{C-D}{2}$$ and similarly for $\sin C - \sin D$, $\cos C \pm \cos D$. Factoring sums is how trig series telescoped in JEE.

nodes.label: Product-to-Sum Formulas
nodes.note: $$2\sin A \cos B = \sin(A+B) + \sin(A-B)$$ $$2\cos A \cos B = \cos(A+B) + \cos(A-B)$$. Multiplication terms collapse into sums, easing integration-style algebra.

nodes.label: Multiple and Sub-Multiple Angles
nodes.note: Double, triple, and half-angle relations plus special products.

nodes.label: Double Angle Relations
nodes.note: $$\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta, \ \cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta, \ \tan 2\theta = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta}$$. Half-angle forms come from reversing them.

nodes.label: Triple Angle Relations
nodes.note: $$\sin 3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta, \ \cos 3\theta = 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta$$. Factor these as cubics in $\sin$ or $\cos$ for equations.

nodes.label: Symmetrical Triplet Product
nodes.note: $$\cos\theta \cos(60^\circ - \theta)\cos(60^\circ + \theta) = \frac{1}{4}\cos 3\theta$$. A frequently regurgitated JEE identity for max-min on trig products.

nodes.label: Half-Angle Substitutions
nodes.note: $$\sin \theta = \frac{2t}{1+t^2}, \ \cos \theta = \frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}, \ t = \tan(\theta/2)$$. The t-substitution rationalizes trig equations.

nodes.label: Conditional Identities in a Triangle
nodes.note: When $A + B + C = \pi$, special relations between the angles appear.

nodes.label: Linear Conditional Identity
nodes.note: If $A + B + C = \pi$: $$\sin A + \sin B + \sin C = 4\cos\frac{A}{2}\cos\frac{B}{2}\cos\frac{C}{2}$$. Sum-to-product on two terms starts the proof.

nodes.label: Tangent Conditional Identity
nodes.note: In a triangle: $$\tan A + \tan B + \tan C = \tan A \tan B \tan C$$. Also $\tan\frac{A}{2}\tan\frac{B}{2} + \tan\frac{B}{2}\tan\frac{C}{2} + \tan\frac{C}{2}\tan\frac{A}{2} = 1$.

nodes.label: Cosine Conditional Identity
nodes.note: In a triangle: $$\cos A + \cos B + \cos C = 1 + 4\sin\frac{A}{2}\sin\frac{B}{2}\sin\frac{C}{2}$$. This converts a cosine sum into a product of half-angle sines.

nodes.label: Trigonometric Equations
nodes.note: General solutions and the linear-equation trick.

nodes.label: Standard General Solutions
nodes.note: $$\sin \theta = \sin \alpha \Rightarrow \theta = n\pi + (-1)^n \alpha$$ $$\cos \theta = \cos \alpha \Rightarrow \theta = 2n\pi \pm \alpha$$ $$\tan \theta = \tan \alpha \Rightarrow \theta = n\pi + \alpha$$. All n are integers.

nodes.label: Linear Equation a cos + b sin = c
nodes.note: Divide by $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ and write as $\cos(\theta - \alpha) = c/\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ where $\tan \alpha = b/a$. Solvability needs $|c| \le \sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

nodes.label: Cofunction Identities
nodes.note: Complementary angles swap sine and cosine: $$\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \cos \theta, \ \tan\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right) = \cot \theta$$. Used when two angles in a problem sum to $\pi/2$.

nodes.label: Example: General Solution
nodes.note: $\sin 2\theta = \sin \theta$ gives $2\theta = n\pi + (-1)^n \theta$, splitting into $\theta = 2n\pi/3$ or $\theta = \pi + 2n\pi$.

nodes.label: Height and Distance
nodes.note: Angles of elevation and depression with sine and cosine rules.

nodes.label: Angle of Elevation
nodes.note: The angle between the horizontal and the line of sight to an object above. With height h and base distance d: $$\tan \alpha = \frac{h}{d}$$. Theodolite problems always start with a right triangle.

nodes.label: Angle of Depression
nodes.note: The angle between the horizontal and the line of sight to an object below. By alternate interior angles, depression from A to B equals elevation from B to A.

nodes.label: Example: Tower and Shadow
nodes.note: A tower casts a shadow of length 20 m at elevation $60^\circ$: $h = 20 \tan 60^\circ = 20\sqrt{3}$ m.

nodes.label: Sine and Cosine Rules in Triangulation
nodes.note: For oblique triangles: $$\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C} = 2R$$ and $$c^2 = a^2 + b^2 - 2ab\cos C$$. Use when the pole leans or the two stations are not level.

nodes.label: Max-Min and Series
nodes.note: Boundedness of trig expressions and arithmetic-angle series.

nodes.label: Max of a sin + b cos
nodes.note: $$a\sin\theta + b\cos\theta \in [-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}, \ \sqrt{a^2+b^2}]$$. This single bound answers most 'range of expression' questions.

nodes.label: Quadratic Trig Forms
nodes.note: Rewrite $a\sin^2\theta + b\sin\theta\cos\theta + c\cos^2\theta$ using double-angle identities to separate a constant and a single $\sin 2\theta / \cos 2\theta$ term.

nodes.label: Example: Range via Bound
nodes.note: The range of $f(\theta) = 3\sin\theta + 4\cos\theta$ is $[-5, 5]$ since $\sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$, so no solving of the equation is needed.

nodes.label: Sine and Cosine Series in AP
nodes.note: $$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \sin(a + kd) = \frac{\sin(nd/2)}{\sin(d/2)} \sin\left(a + \frac{(n-1)d}{2}\right)$$. Multiply and divide by $2\sin(d/2)$ to get a telescoping product-to-sum series.

nodes.label: Vectors and 3D Geometry
nodes.note: Vector algebra extends dot and cross products to three dimensions, and 3D geometry uses them to describe lines, planes, angles, and distances in space. The two products that drive everything are $$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \cos\theta$$ and $$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin\theta \, \hat{n}$$.

nodes.label: Vector Algebra
nodes.note: A vector in space is written $$\vec{a} = a_1 \hat{i} + a_2 \hat{j} + a_3 \hat{k}$$ with magnitude $$|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}$$. The dot product returns a scalar while the cross product returns a vector perpendicular to both operands.

nodes.label: Vector Basics and Representation
nodes.note: A vector has magnitude and direction, resolved into components along $$\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$$. Its magnitude is $$|\vec{a}| = \sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}$$ and the direction cosines are the cosines of the angles it makes with the three axes.

nodes.label: Unit Vector
nodes.note: A unit vector has magnitude one and points along a given direction, computed as $$\hat{a} = \frac{\vec{a}}{|\vec{a}|}$$. The standard unit vectors $$\hat{i}, \hat{j}, \hat{k}$$ are mutually perpendicular with $$\hat{i} \cdot \hat{i} = 1$$ and $$\hat{i} \cdot \hat{j} = 0$$.

nodes.label: Position and Free Vectors
nodes.note: The position vector of a point $$P$$ is the vector $$\overrightarrow{OP}$$ from the origin to $$P$$, fixing its location in space. A free vector is independent of its starting point and is fully described by its components and magnitude.

nodes.label: Addition and Scalar Multiplication
nodes.note: Vectors add by the triangle or parallelogram law and scale by multiplying each component, giving $$(a_1 + b_1)\hat{i} + (a_2 + b_2)\hat{j} + (a_3 + b_3)\hat{k}$$. Addition is commutative and the zero vector is the identity.

nodes.label: Dot Product
nodes.note: The dot product is $$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \cos\theta = a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3$$, a scalar that is positive for acute and negative for obtuse angles. It also equals $$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{a} = |\vec{a}|^2$$, which gives magnitudes without square roots.

nodes.label: Angle Between Vectors
nodes.note: The angle between two nonzero vectors is $$\cos\theta = \frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{a}| |\vec{b}|} = \frac{a_1 b_1 + a_2 b_2 + a_3 b_3}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + a_2^2 + a_3^2}\sqrt{b_1^2 + b_2^2 + b_3^2}}$$. The absolute value is taken when only the acute angle is required.

nodes.label: Projection of a Vector
nodes.note: The scalar projection of $$\vec{a}$$ onto $$\vec{b}$$ is $$\frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|}$$ and the vector projection is $$\frac{\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}}{|\vec{b}|^2}\,\vec{b}$$. Projection onto a unit vector is simply the dot product with that unit vector.

nodes.label: Perpendicular Vectors
nodes.note: Two vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product vanishes, $$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = 0$$, since $$\cos 90^\circ = 0$$. This is the cleanest test for orthogonality and is used to build vectors normal to a plane.

nodes.label: Dot Product Properties
nodes.note: The dot product is commutative, $$\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} = \vec{b} \cdot \vec{a}$$, and distributive, $$\vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} + \vec{c}) = \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b} + \vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}$$. It is not associative because the dot product of two vectors is a scalar, not a vector.

nodes.label: Cross Product
nodes.note: The cross product is $$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin\theta \, \hat{n}$$, a vector perpendicular to both $$\vec{a}$$ and $$\vec{b}$$ by the right-hand rule. In components it is the determinant $$\begin{vmatrix} \hat{i} & \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}$$.

nodes.label: Cross Product Properties
nodes.note: The cross product is anti-commutative, $$\vec{a} \times \vec{b} = -\vec{b} \times \vec{a}$$, and vanishes for parallel vectors, $$\vec{a} \times \vec{a} = 0$$. It is distributive over addition but not associative in general.

nodes.label: Unit Vector Perpendicular to Two Vectors
nodes.note: A unit vector perpendicular to both $$\vec{a}$$ and $$\vec{b}$$ is $$\hat{n} = \pm \frac{\vec{a} \times \vec{b}}{|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|}$$, with the sign choosing the orientation. The magnitude $$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$$ equals the area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors.

nodes.label: Geometric Meaning of the Cross Product
nodes.note: The magnitude $$|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}| = |\vec{a}| |\vec{b}| \sin\theta$$ is the area of the parallelogram on $$\vec{a}$$ and $$\vec{b}$$, so the triangle on them has area $$\frac{1}{2}|\vec{a} \times \vec{b}|$$. Its direction is the normal to the plane containing the two vectors.

nodes.label: Triple Products
nodes.note: Triple products combine three vectors into a scalar or a vector and carry the geometry of volume and coplanarity. The two of them are the scalar triple product $$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]$$ and the vector triple product $$\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$$.

nodes.label: Scalar Triple Product
nodes.note: The scalar triple product is $$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c})$$, a scalar equal to the determinant of the components. Its absolute value is the volume of the parallelepiped, $$V = |[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]|$$.

nodes.label: Coplanarity of Vectors
nodes.note: Three vectors are coplanar exactly when their scalar triple product is zero, $$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = 0$$, because the parallelepiped they span has zero volume. This is the standard test for whether three vectors, or four points, lie in a common plane.

nodes.label: Properties of the Scalar Triple Product
nodes.note: The dot and cross may be interchanged, $$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = \vec{a} \cdot (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = (\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \cdot \vec{c}$$, and it is cyclic, $$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = [\vec{b} \, \vec{c} \, \vec{a}] = [\vec{c} \, \vec{a} \, \vec{b}]$$. Swapping two vectors reverses the sign, so $$[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}] = -[\vec{a} \, \vec{c} \, \vec{b}]$$.

nodes.label: Volume of a Tetrahedron
nodes.note: The volume of a tetrahedron on three coterminous edges $$\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$$ is one sixth of the parallelepiped volume, $$V_{\text{tetra}} = \frac{1}{6}[\vec{a} \, \vec{b} \, \vec{c}]$$. It vanishes when the four vertices are coplanar, matching the scalar triple product test.

nodes.label: Vector Triple Product
nodes.note: The vector triple product expands by the BAC-CAB rule, $$\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \vec{b}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}) - \vec{c}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})$$. The result lies in the plane of $$\vec{b}$$ and $$\vec{c}$$ and is perpendicular to $$\vec{a}$$.

nodes.label: The BAC-CAB Identity
nodes.note: The identity $$\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) = \vec{b}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{c}) - \vec{c}(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b})$$ is remembered as BAC minus CAB because the outer vector $$\vec{a}$$ dots with the far vector in each term. It is not associative, so $$\vec{a} \times (\vec{b} \times \vec{c}) \neq (\vec{a} \times \vec{b}) \times \vec{c}$$ in general.

nodes.label: Direction Cosines and Ratios
nodes.note: Direction cosines $$l, m, n$$ are the cosines of the angles a line makes with the positive $$x, y, z$$ axes and satisfy $$l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$$. Direction ratios are any triple proportional to them and fix the same direction.

nodes.label: Direction Cosines
nodes.note: For a line making angles $$\alpha, \beta, \gamma$$ with the axes the direction cosines are $$l = \cos\alpha, m = \cos\beta, n = \cos\gamma$$ and always obey $$l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$$. A line has two opposite sets of direction cosines corresponding to its two directions.

nodes.label: Direction Cosines from Ratios
nodes.note: If $$a, b, c$$ are direction ratios then the direction cosines are $$l = \frac{\pm a}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}, m = \frac{\pm b}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}, n = \frac{\pm c}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$$, with a consistent choice of sign. Any nonzero multiple of a set of direction ratios gives the same direction cosines up to sign.

nodes.label: Direction Cosines of a Line Joining Two Points
nodes.note: For the segment joining $$P(x_1, y_1, z_1)$$ and $$Q(x_2, y_2, z_2)$$ the direction cosines are $$l = \frac{x_2 - x_1}{PQ}, m = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{PQ}, n = \frac{z_2 - z_1}{PQ}$$ where $$PQ = \sqrt{(x_2 - x_1)^2 + (y_2 - y_1)^2 + (z_2 - z_1)^2}$$. These are simply the components of the unit vector along the segment.

nodes.label: Direction Cosine Identities
nodes.note: From $$l^2 + m^2 + n^2 = 1$$ it follows that $$\sin^2\alpha + \sin^2\beta + \sin^2\gamma = 2$$ and $$\cos 2\alpha + \cos 2\beta + \cos 2\gamma = -1$$. These identities let one direction cosine be found from the other two.

nodes.label: Direction Ratios
nodes.note: Direction ratios $$a, b, c$$ are any numbers proportional to the direction cosines, so $$a : b : c = l : m : n$$. They are not unique since multiplying by any nonzero constant gives the same direction, which is why one normalizes to get cosines.

nodes.label: Proportionality of Ratios and Cosines
nodes.note: If $$a, b, c$$ are direction ratios and $$l, m, n$$ are direction cosines then $$\frac{l}{a} = \frac{m}{b} = \frac{n}{c} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$$ up to sign. This proportionality is the bridge used to convert between the two notations in every 3D problem.

nodes.label: Angle Between Two Lines
nodes.note: Using direction ratios the acute angle between two lines is $$\cos\theta = \frac{|a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 + c_1 c_2|}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2}\sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}}$$, and with direction cosines it is $$\cos\theta = |l_1 l_2 + m_1 m_2 + n_1 n_2|$$. The absolute value forces the acute angle.

nodes.label: Parallel and Perpendicular Lines
nodes.note: Two lines are parallel when their direction ratios are proportional, $$\frac{a_1}{a_2} = \frac{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{c_1}{c_2}$$, and perpendicular when the dot product of their direction vectors is zero, $$a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 + c_1 c_2 = 0$$. In direction cosines the perpendicular test is simply $$l_1 l_2 + m_1 m_2 + n_1 n_2 = 0$$.

nodes.label: Lines in Space
nodes.note: A line in space is fixed by a point and a direction, giving the vector form $$\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda \vec{b}$$ and the Cartesian form $$\frac{x - x_1}{a} = \frac{y - y_1}{b} = \frac{z - z_1}{c}$$. Distances and angles between lines follow from their direction vectors.

nodes.label: Equation of a Line
nodes.note: A line through the point with position vector $$\vec{a}$$ and parallel to $$\vec{b}$$ is $$\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda \vec{b}$$, or in Cartesian form $$\frac{x - x_1}{a} = \frac{y - y_1}{b} = \frac{z - z_1}{c}$$ where $$a, b, c$$ are direction ratios. Each value of $$\lambda$$ gives one point of the line.

nodes.label: Line Through Two Points
nodes.note: The line through points with position vectors $$\vec{a}$$ and $$\vec{b}$$ is $$\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda(\vec{b} - \vec{a})$$, since $$\vec{b} - \vec{a}$$ is a direction vector. In Cartesian form the direction ratios are just the differences of the coordinates of the two points.

nodes.label: Cartesian and Vector Forms
nodes.note: The Cartesian form $$\frac{x - x_1}{a} = \frac{y - y_1}{b} = \frac{z - z_1}{c} = \lambda$$ is converted to vector form by reading the point $$(x_1, y_1, z_1)$$ as $$\vec{a}$$ and the denominators as $$\vec{b}$$. The two forms are equivalent and one switches between them freely in JEE.

nodes.label: Parametric Coordinates of a Line
nodes.note: Writing the line as $$x = x_1 + a\lambda, y = y_1 + b\lambda, z = z_1 + c\lambda$$ gives a point for every value of the parameter $$\lambda$$. Substituting these into a plane equation yields the single $$\lambda$$ at which the line meets the plane.

nodes.label: Shortest Distance Between Skew Lines
nodes.note: Skew lines are neither parallel nor intersecting, and the shortest distance between $$\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda \vec{b}_1$$ and $$\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu \vec{b}_2$$ is $$SD = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2)|}{|\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2|}$$. The numerator is a scalar triple product and the denominator is the area of the base.

nodes.label: Distance Between Parallel Lines
nodes.note: For parallel lines $$\vec{r} = \vec{a}_1 + \lambda \vec{b}$$ and $$\vec{r} = \vec{a}_2 + \mu \vec{b}$$ the shortest distance is $$d = \frac{|(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \times \vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$$, the length of the perpendicular between them. This is the projection of the join onto the common perpendicular direction.

nodes.label: Coplanarity of Two Lines
nodes.note: Two lines are coplanar, i.e. lie in a common plane, exactly when $$(\vec{a}_2 - \vec{a}_1) \cdot (\vec{b}_1 \times \vec{b}_2) = 0$$, meaning the join of the points is perpendicular to the common perpendicular. Equivalently the scalar triple product of the join and the two direction vectors vanishes, which is also the condition for the lines to intersect.

nodes.label: Intersection of Two Lines
nodes.note: Two lines intersect when they are coplanar and not parallel, and the point is found by equating the parametric coordinates $$\vec{a}_1 + \lambda \vec{b}_1 = \vec{a}_2 + \mu \vec{b}_2$$ and solving for $$\lambda$$ and $$\mu$$. If the resulting values satisfy all three coordinate equations simultaneously the lines meet at a single point.

nodes.label: Distance of a Point from a Line
nodes.note: The perpendicular distance of a point with position vector $$\vec{c}$$ from the line through $$\vec{a}$$ with direction $$\vec{b}$$ is $$d = \frac{|(\vec{c} - \vec{a}) \times \vec{b}|}{|\vec{b}|}$$. It is the height of the parallelogram on $$\vec{c} - \vec{a}$$ and $$\vec{b}$$, giving the shortest gap to the line.

nodes.label: Planes
nodes.note: A plane is fixed by a point and a normal vector, giving the vector form $$\vec{r} \cdot \hat{n} = d$$ and the Cartesian form $$ax + by + cz + d = 0$$ where $$a, b, c$$ are direction ratios of the normal. Angles and distances involving planes reduce to the normal.

nodes.label: Equation of a Plane
nodes.note: The plane through the point with position vector $$\vec{a}$$ and normal $$\vec{n}$$ is $$\vec{n} \cdot (\vec{r} - \vec{a}) = 0$$, or $$\vec{r} \cdot \hat{n} = d$$ in unit-normal form, or $$ax + by + cz + d = 0$$ in Cartesian form. The coefficients $$a, b, c$$ are the direction ratios of the normal.

nodes.label: Plane Through Three Points
nodes.note: The plane through three non-collinear points with position vectors $$\vec{a}, \vec{b}, \vec{c}$$ has normal $$(\vec{b} - \vec{a}) \times (\vec{c} - \vec{a})$$, so its equation is $$(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot [(\vec{b} - \vec{a}) \times (\vec{c} - \vec{a})] = 0$$. The cross product supplies a vector perpendicular to both in-plane edges.

nodes.label: Plane Through a Line and a Point
nodes.note: A plane containing the line $$\vec{r} = \vec{a} + \lambda \vec{b}$$ and an external point $$\vec{c}$$ has normal $$\vec{b} \times (\vec{c} - \vec{a})$$ and equation $$(\vec{r} - \vec{a}) \cdot [\vec{b} \times (\vec{c} - \vec{a})] = 0$$. The normal is perpendicular to both the line direction and the join to the external point.

nodes.label: Normal Form and Distance from Origin
nodes.note: Dividing $$ax + by + cz + d = 0$$ by $$\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}$$ gives the normal form $$\vec{r} \cdot \hat{n} = p$$ where $$p$$ is the perpendicular distance of the plane from the origin. The unit normal is $$\hat{n} = \frac{a\hat{i} + b\hat{j} + c\hat{k}}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$$.

nodes.label: Angle Between Two Planes
nodes.note: The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals, so for $$a_1 x + b_1 y + c_1 z + d_1 = 0$$ and $$a_2 x + b_2 y + c_2 z + d_2 = 0$$ it is $$\cos\theta = \frac{|a_1 a_2 + b_1 b_2 + c_1 c_2|}{\sqrt{a_1^2 + b_1^2 + c_1^2}\sqrt{a_2^2 + b_2^2 + c_2^2}}$$. The planes are perpendicular when this dot product is zero.

nodes.label: Angle Between a Line and a Plane
nodes.note: If a line has direction ratios $$l, m, n$$ and the plane has normal $$a, b, c$$, the angle between the line and the plane is $$\sin\theta = \frac{|al + bm + cn|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}\sqrt{l^2 + m^2 + n^2}}$$. The sine appears because the angle is measured from the plane, i.e. it is the complement of the angle to the normal.

nodes.label: Line Parallel and Perpendicular to a Plane
nodes.note: A line is parallel to a plane when its direction is perpendicular to the normal, $$al + bm + cn = 0$$, and perpendicular to the plane when its direction is parallel to the normal, $$\frac{l}{a} = \frac{m}{b} = \frac{n}{c}$$. A line lies in the plane when it is parallel to it and one of its points satisfies the plane equation.

nodes.label: Distance of a Point from a Plane
nodes.note: The perpendicular distance of the point $$(x_1, y_1, z_1)$$ from the plane $$ax + by + cz + d = 0$$ is $$d = \frac{|ax_1 + by_1 + cz_1 + d|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}$$. The sign of the numerator indicates on which side of the plane the point lies.

nodes.label: Image of a Point in a Plane
nodes.note: The image of a point in a plane is found by dropping the perpendicular, doubling it, and stepping to the far side, exactly as for a line mirror in two dimensions. If $$P$$ is at signed distance $$\delta$$ from the plane along the unit normal, the image is $$P - 2\delta \hat{n}$$, and the foot is the midpoint of the point and its image.

nodes.label: Family of Planes
nodes.note: The planes through the intersection of two planes $$P_1 = 0$$ and $$P_2 = 0$$ form the family $$P_1 + \lambda P_2 = 0$$ for any real $$\lambda$$. Fixing $$\lambda$$ by requiring the member to pass through a given point selects the unique plane of the family through that point.

nodes.label: Inorganic Chemistry
nodes.note: Complete JEE Main inorganic roadmap: periodicity, s/p/d/f blocks, hydrogen, bonding, equilibrium, redox, electrochemistry, coordination compounds, metallurgy, qualitative analysis and environmental chemistry. Nodes group every pillar chapter, its core trends and the named tests/reagents asked in PYQs.

nodes.label: Periodic Table and Periodicity
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Periodic Table and Periodicity. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Electronic Configuration and Blocks
nodes.note: Every element's block is fixed by its valence subshell: $$ns^{1-2}$$ is s-block, $$ns^2np^{1-6}$$ is p-block, $$(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}$$ is d-block, and $$(n-2)f^{0-14}$$ is f-block. Expect questions on which orbital holds the differentiating electron.

nodes.label: Atomic and Ionic Radius
nodes.note: Radius decreases across a period (rising $$Z_{eff}$$) and increases down a group. Cations shrink: $$Na^+ < Na$$; anions expand: $$Cl^- > Cl$$. Isoelectronic size order: $$N^{3-} > O^{2-} > F^- > Na^+ > Mg^{2+} > Al^{3+}$$.

nodes.label: Ionisation Enthalpy
nodes.note: Energy to remove the most loosely held electron: $$M(g) \rightarrow M^+(g) + e^-$$. IE rises across a period and falls down a group; successive IEs $$IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3$$ jump when a noble-gas core is broken.

nodes.label: IE Exceptions (N>O, Be>B, Mg>Al)
nodes.note: Half-filled and fully-filled subshells are extra stable, so $$N > O$$ (N has $$2p^3$$) and $$Be > B$$, $$Mg > Al$$. A JEE classic trap: although IE generally increases across a period, these two dips recur every period.

nodes.label: Electron Gain Enthalpy
nodes.note: Energy change on adding an electron: $$X(g) + e^- \rightarrow X^-(g)$$. It usually becomes more negative across a period, but Cl has the most negative EGE, not F, because tiny $$F^-$$ suffers lone-pair repulsion.

nodes.label: Electronegativity
nodes.note: Pauling's scale measures an atom's electron-pulling power; F (4.0) is the maximum and decreases down a group and increases across a period. It predicts bond polarity and whether a hydride is ionic or covalent.

nodes.label: Metallic and Non-metallic Character
nodes.note: Metallic character (ease of losing electrons) increases down a group and decreases across a period, opposite to non-metallic character. Highest metallic: Fr/Cs; highest non-metallic: F.

nodes.label: Periodicity of Oxidation States
nodes.note: Maximum oxidation state often equals the group number through $$+7$$, then falls after Mn: $$Cr^{+6}$$, $$Mn^{+7}$$ in $$KMnO_4$$, $$Fe^{+6}$$ in $$K_2FeO_4$$. Lower states stabilise down a group (inert pair effect, later).

nodes.label: S Block Elements
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: S Block Elements. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Group 1: Alkali Metals
nodes.note: Soft, low-melting metals with configuration $$ns^1$$: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr. Very low IE makes them powerful reducing agents; hydration enthalpy of $$Li^+$$ is the largest in the group.

nodes.label: Oxides, Peroxides, Superoxides
nodes.note: Combustion in air gives oxides (Li: $$Li_2O$$), peroxides (Na: $$Na_2O_2$$) and superoxides (K, Rb, Cs: $$KO_2$$). Superoxides like $$KO_2$$ liberate $$O_2$$, used in submarine air supply: $$4KO_2 + 2CO_2 \rightarrow 2K_2CO_3 + 3O_2$$.

nodes.label: Solution in Liquid NH3 (Blue)
nodes.note: Dissolved alkali metals give a deep blue paramagnetic solution from solvated electrons: $$M + (x+y)NH_3 \rightarrow [M(NH_3)_x]^+ + [e(NH_3)_y]^-$$. On standing it decomposes to $$NaNH_2$$ plus $$H_2$$.

nodes.label: Group 2: Alkaline Earth Metals
nodes.note: Harder, denser metals $$ns^2$$: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra. Solubility of hydroxides rises down the group while solubility of sulfates falls: $$BeSO_4, MgSO_4$$ soluble, $$BaSO_4$$ insoluble.

nodes.label: Anomalous Be and Mg
nodes.note: Small Be shows covalent character: $$BeCl_2$$ is polymeric and $$BeCO_3$$ is unstable; Mg forms a nitride $$Mg_3N_2$$ unlike other group members and its carbonate decomposes most easily. These are fixed JEE favourites.

nodes.label: Diagonal Relationship (Li-Mg, Be-Al)
nodes.note: Li resembles Mg and Be resembles Al: similar polarising power gives amphoteric hydroxides, covalent chlorides and nitride formation. Example: both Li and Mg form nitrides, $$Li_3N$$ and $$Mg_3N_2$$, on heating in air.

nodes.label: Flame Test Colors (s-Block)
nodes.note: Characteristic flame emission: Li crimson red, Na golden yellow, K lilac (violet), Ca brick red, Sr crimson red, Ba apple green. Be and Mg show no characteristic flame since their excitation energies lie in the UV.

nodes.label: Thermal Stability of Carbonates and Nitrates
nodes.note: Stability of carbonates and nitrates increases down a group because the larger cation polarises the anion less: $$MCO_3 \rightarrow MO + CO_2$$, $$2MNO_3 \rightarrow 2MNO_2 + O_2$$. $$Li_2CO_3$$ and $$LiNO_3$$ decompose most easily in Group 1.

nodes.label: Important Sodium Compounds
nodes.note: NaOH (caustic soda, Castner-Kellner cell), $$Na_2CO_3$$ (washing soda, Solvay process) and $$NaHCO_3$$ (baking soda, mild) dominate JEE. $$Na_2CO_3$$ on heating does not decompose (unlike $$Li_2CO_3$$).

nodes.label: Solvay Process for Na2CO3
nodes.note: Industrial preparation: $$NaCl + NH_3 + CO_2 + H_2O \rightarrow NaHCO_3 + NH_4Cl$$, then $$2NaHCO_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} Na_2CO_3 + CO_2 + H_2O$$. Note $$K_2CO_3$$ cannot be made this way because $$KHCO_3$$ is too soluble.

nodes.label: Important Calcium Compounds
nodes.note: Key substances: quicklime $$CaO$$, slaked lime $$Ca(OH)_2$$, lime water, bleaching powder $$CaOCl_2$$, and plaster of Paris $$CaSO_4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}H_2O$$. Setting of POP is crystallisation of gypsum: $$CaSO_4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}H_2O + \tfrac{3}{2}H_2O \rightarrow CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O$$.

nodes.label: P Block Elements
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: P Block Elements. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Group 13: Boron Family
nodes.note: Boron is a metalloid with electron-deficient $$BCl_3$$; Al is amphoteric: $$Al_2O_3 + 2NaOH \rightarrow 2NaAlO_2 + H_2O$$. Gallium, indium and thallium show increasing inert-pair stability of the $$+1$$ state down the group.

nodes.label: Group 14: Carbon Family
nodes.note: C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb with states $$+4$$ and $$+2$$; stability of $$+2$$ grows down the group (inert pair effect). $$CO_2$$ is a gas while $$SiO_2$$ is a giant covalent solid; watch oxidation states: $$PbO_2$$ is a strong oxidiser, $$PbCl_4$$ unstable.

nodes.label: Group 15: Nitrogen Family
nodes.note: N, P, As, Sb, Bi. Nitrogen shows $$p\pi-p\pi$$ back-bonding ($$N_2$$, $$N_2O$$, NO) unlike heavier congeners. $$NH_3$$ is basic, $$HNO_3$$ is a strong oxidising acid, and $$PCl_5$$ exists while $$NCl_5$$ does not (no d-orbitals).

nodes.label: Haber Process for Ammonia
nodes.note: Industrial synthesis: $$N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)$$, exothermic, favoured by high pressure ~200 atm and Fe catalyst with Mo promoter. A high-pressure, moderately heated equilibrium compromise.

nodes.label: Oxoacids of Nitrogen
nodes.note: Key acids: $$HNO_2$$ (nitrous, unstable), $$HNO_3$$ (nitric), $$H_2N_2O_2$$ (hyponitrous). Basicity = number of $$-OH$$ groups; $$H_3PO_2$$ and $$H_3PO_3$$ are reducing, $$HNO_3$$ oxidising.

nodes.label: Group 16: Oxygen Family
nodes.note: O, S, Se, Te, Po. $$O_3$$ (ozone) is a bent triatomic allotrope: $$2O_3 \rightarrow 3O_2$$. Sulfur's acids dominate: $$H_2SO_4$$ (contact process, strong dehydrating agent) and $$H_2S_2O_8$$ (peroxodisulfuric, has $$-O-O-$$ linkage).

nodes.label: Contact Process for H2SO4
nodes.note: Sulfur burned to $$SO_2$$, catalytically oxidised: $$2SO_2 + O_2 \rightleftharpoons[V_2O_5]{} 2SO_3$$, then absorbed in $$H_2SO_4$$ to give oleum $$H_2S_2O_7$$, diluted to $$H_2SO_4$$.

nodes.label: Ozone Layer Chemistry
nodes.note: CFCs release Cl radicals that destroy ozone: $$Cl + O_3 \rightarrow ClO + O_2$$, $$ClO + O \rightarrow Cl + O_2$$. This radical chain thins the stratospheric ozone layer, increasing harmful UV-B at the surface.

nodes.label: Group 17: Halogens
nodes.note: F, Cl, Br, I with configuration $$ns^2np^5$$. Bond dissociation anomaly: $$F_2$$ has lower bond energy than $$Cl_2$$ due to lone-pair repulsion. All form $$HX$$; $$HF$$ is the weakest acid yet forms $$HF_2^-$$ ($$F^- \cdots HF$$).

nodes.label: Halogen Oxoacids
nodes.note: Order of acid strength $$HOCl < HClO_2 < HClO_3 < HClO_4$$; oxidising power decreases down the order. $$HClO_4$$ is the strongest halogen acid; perhalates are powerful oxidisers.

nodes.label: Group 18: Noble Gases
nodes.note: He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe, Rn with closed shells $$ns^2np^6$$ (He: $$1s^2$$). Only heavier noble gases form compounds: $$XeF_2$$ (linear), $$XeF_4$$ (square planar), $$XeO_3$$ (pyramidal) via VSEPR with lone pairs.

nodes.label: Xenon Fluorides (XeF2, XeF4, XeF6)
nodes.note: Direct fluorination: $$Xe + F_2 \xrightarrow{Ni, 673K} XeF_2$$, $$Xe + 2F_2 \xrightarrow{Ni, 873K} XeF_4$$, $$Xe + 3F_2 \xrightarrow{Ni, 1173K} XeF_6$$. Hydrolysis of $$XeF_6$$: $$XeF_6 + H_2O \rightarrow XeOF_4 + 2HF$$.

nodes.label: Inert Pair Effect
nodes.note: Down groups 13-15 the $$ns^2$$ pair resists bonding, stabilising lower oxidation states: $$Tl^+ > Tl^{3+}$$, $$Pb^{2+} > Pb^{4+}$$, $$Bi^{3+} > Bi^{5+}$$. A direct periodicity consequence examiners love.

nodes.label: Hydrogen
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Hydrogen. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Isotopes and Preparation of H2
nodes.note: Protium $$^1H$$, deuterium $$^2H$$ (D), radioactive tritium $$^3H$$. Lab preparation: $$Zn + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2$$; large scale via steam reforming: $$CH_4 + H_2O \xrightarrow{1273K} CO + 3H_2$$.

nodes.label: Water Gas Shift Reaction
nodes.note: To increase $$H_2$$ yield, CO in water gas is shifted: $$CO + H_2O \xrightarrow{673K} CO_2 + H_2$$. Iron-chrome or copper-zinc oxide catalysts are used industrially.

nodes.label: Types of Hydrides
nodes.note: Ionic (saline): $$NaH, CaH_2$$; covalent: $$CH_4, NH_3, H_2O, HF$$; interstitial (metallic): non-stoichiometric, e.g. $$PdH_{0.6}$$, electrically conducting. Trend in boiling points: $$H_2O$$ anomalously high due to H-bonding.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Peroxide (H2O2)
nodes.note: Prepared by anthraquinone process; structure has $$-O-O-$$ bridge: $$H-O-O-H$$ with dihedral angle ~109.8 deg in gas. $$H_2O_2$$ acts as both oxidiser and reducer: $$H_2O_2 + 2KI \rightarrow 2KOH + I_2$$, $$H_2O_2 + Ag_2O \rightarrow 2Ag + H_2O + O_2$$.

nodes.label: Structure and Bond Angle of H2O2
nodes.note: Open book (skewed) structure with O-O single bond; gas dihedral 111.5 deg, crystalline altered by H-bonding. Oxidation state of O is $$-1$$, between $$-2$$ (water) and $$0$$ ($$O_2$$).

nodes.label: Water and Heavy Water
nodes.note: $$H_2O$$ is a bent molecule ($$\angle H-O-H \approx 104.5^\circ$$) with strong H-bonding giving high boiling point. Heavy water $$D_2O$$ is used as a moderator in nuclear reactors and in NMR/tracer studies.

nodes.label: D and F Block Elements
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: D and F Block Elements. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: General Properties of d-Block
nodes.note: Transition metals show variable oxidation states, coloured ions, paramagnetism and catalytic activity. Config: $$(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{1-2}$$ with the exception of $$Cr: [Ar]3d^54s^1$$ and $$Cu: [Ar]3d^{10}4s^1$$.

nodes.label: Oxidation States and Trends
nodes.note: Max oxidation state peaks at group 7: $$Mn^{+7}$$ in $$Mn_2O_7$$; $$Sc^{+3}$$ and $$Zn^{+2}$$ are common. High states are oxidising ($$Cr_2O_7^{2-}$$), low states often reducing ($$V^{2+}$$).

nodes.label: Spin-Only Magnetic Moment
nodes.note: For unpaired electrons n: $$\mu_{so} = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$$ BM. Used to count d-electrons, e.g. $$Fe^{3+}$$ (d5): $$\mu = \sqrt{5 \cdot 7} = 5.92$$ BM.

nodes.label: Lanthanoid Contraction
nodes.note: Poor shielding by 4f electrons shrinks radii across the lanthanoids: $$La^{3+}$$ (106 pm) to $$Lu^{3+}$$ (85 pm). Consequence: 4d and 5d pairs (Zr/Hf, Nb/Ta, Mo/W) have nearly equal radii and chemistry.

nodes.label: Important d-Block Compounds
nodes.note: $$KMnO_4$$ (purple, strong oxidiser), $$K_2Cr_2O_7$$ (orange, oxidiser in acid), $$K_2CrO_4$$ (yellow), and $$FeSO_4 \cdot (NH_4)_2SO_4 \cdot 6H_2O$$ (Mohr's salt). Colour: $$MnO_4^-$$ purple, $$CrO_4^{2-}$$ yellow, $$Cr_2O_7^{2-}$$ orange.

nodes.label: KMnO4 as Oxidant
nodes.note: In acid: $$MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \rightarrow Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O$$ (purple to colourless). In neutral/alkaline medium it reduces to $$MnO_2$$: $$MnO_4^- + 2H_2O + 3e^- \rightarrow MnO_2 + 4OH^-$$.

nodes.label: Cr2O7^2- / CrO4^2- Equilibrium
nodes.note: $$Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 2OH^- \rightleftharpoons 2CrO_4^{2-} + H_2O$$. Orange dichromate in acid, yellow chromate in base - classic Le Chatelier demo.

nodes.label: Transition Metal Catalysts
nodes.note: Fe (Haber, with Mo promoter), $$V_2O_5$$ (contact), Ni (hydrogenation), Pt/Pd (petroleum reforming). Adsorption of reactants on the surface and availability of d-orbitals explain activity.

nodes.label: F-Block: Lanthanoids and Actinoids
nodes.note: Lanthanoids (4f) are silvery, with common state $$+3$$; $$Ce^{4+}$$ and $$Eu^{2+}$$ are notable. Actinoids (5f) are radioactive, all show $$+3$$, and heavier ones have low stability; $$U^{6+}$$ in uranyl $$UO_2^{2+}$$.

nodes.label: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Chemical Bonding and Molecular Structure. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Ionic Bond and Lattice Enthalpy
nodes.note: Formed by electron transfer giving a cation-anion lattice; lattice enthalpy is the energy released when gaseous ions form a solid, $$Na^+(g) + Cl^-(g) \rightarrow NaCl(s)$$. Higher charges and smaller ions give larger lattice enthalpy.

nodes.label: Born-Haber Cycle
nodes.note: Hess-law bookkeeping of formation: $$\Delta H_f = S + \tfrac{1}{2}D + IE + EA - U$$. Lets you estimate lattice energy or electron affinity that cannot be measured directly.

nodes.label: Covalent Bonding and VBT
nodes.note: VBT: bonds form by overlap of half-filled orbitals with paired spins ($$\sigma$$ by head-on, $$\pi$$ by sideways overlap). $$\sigma$$ is stronger than $$\pi$$; $$N_2$$'s triple bond $$N \equiv N$$ has one $$\sigma$$ and two $$\pi$$.

nodes.label: VSEPR Theory and Geometries
nodes.note: Geometry follows electron-pair repulsion: $$AX_2$$ linear, $$AX_3$$ trigonal planar, $$AX_4$$ tetrahedral, $$AX_2E_2$$ bent ($$H_2O$$, 104.5 deg), $$AX_3E$$ pyramidal ($$NH_3$$, 107 deg). Lone pairs compress bond angles.

nodes.label: Hybridization
nodes.note: Mixing of orbitals gives directed geometry: $$sp$$ (linear), $$sp^2$$ (trigonal planar), $$sp^3$$ (tetrahedral), $$dsp^2$$ (square planar), $$sp^3d^2$$ (octahedral). Count $$\sigma$$ bonds + lone pairs to assign.

nodes.label: Molecular Orbital Theory
nodes.note: MOs form by LCAO; for Z <= 7 the order is $$\sigma 1s < \sigma^*1s < \sigma 2s < \sigma^*2s < \pi 2p < \sigma 2p < \pi^*2p < \sigma^*2p$$, and for O, F, Ne the $$\sigma 2p$$ and $$\pi 2p$$ swap. Bond order $$BO = \tfrac{1}{2}(N_b - N_a)$$ sets stability: $$O_2$$ has BO = 2 and is paramagnetic.

nodes.label: Dipole Moment and Molecular Polarity
nodes.note: $$\mu = q \cdot d$$. $$CO_2$$ (linear, two opposing dipoles) has $$\mu = 0$$ though C=O is polar; $$H_2O$$ and $$NH_3$$ are polar. $$NF_3 < NH_3$$ in $$\mu$$ because lone-pair and bond dipoles oppose in $$NF_3$$.

nodes.label: Fajan's Rules of Polarization
nodes.note: Small highly charged cations and large polarisable anions increase covalent character: $$LiI$$ more covalent than $$LiF$$; $$AlCl_3$$ covalent, $$AlF_3$$ ionic. Explains solubility and colour trends.

nodes.label: Hydrogen Bonding
nodes.note: H covalently bound to F/O/N is attracted to a lone pair on F/O/N: $$O-H \cdots O$$. Explains high bp of $$H_2O, HF, NH_3$$ and why ice (open cage) floats: max density of water at 4 deg C.

nodes.label: Open Cage Structure of Ice
nodes.note: Each water in ice H-bonds tetrahedrally to four neighbours, leaving cavities; volume expands on freezing so ice is less dense (0.917 g/cm3) and floats. This is vital for aquatic life in winter.

nodes.label: Intermolecular Forces (vdW)
nodes.note: London dispersion (all molecules, rises with size), dipole-dipole, and H-bonding (strongest). Boiling points: $$He < Ar < Kr$$ from rising dispersion; polar $$HCl$$ boils above non-polar $$F_2$$ of similar mass.

nodes.label: Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Chemical and Ionic Equilibrium. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Equilibrium Constant Kc and Kp
nodes.note: For $$aA + bB \rightleftharpoons cC + dD$$, $$K_c = \frac{[C]^c[D]^d}{[A]^a[B]^b}$$ and $$K_p = K_c(RT)^{\Delta n_g}$$. Solids and pure liquids are omitted. Large K means products dominate at equilibrium.

nodes.label: Le Chatelier's Principle
nodes.note: A system at equilibrium shifts to counter any imposed change. For $$N_2 + 3H_2 \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3$$ ($$\Delta H < 0$$), high pressure and low temperature favour $$NH_3$$; a catalyst only speeds attainment of equilibrium.

nodes.label: Degree of Dissociation
nodes.note: Fraction dissociated $$\alpha$$; for $$N_2O_4 \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2$$, $$K_p = \frac{4\alpha^2 P}{1-\alpha^2}$$. Higher temperature shifts toward more $$NO_2$$ (browner gas) since dissociation is endothermic.

nodes.label: Acids, Bases and pH
nodes.note: $$pH = -\log[H^+]$$, $$pOH = 14 - pH$$ at 25 deg C. Strong acid $$HCl$$: $$pH = -\log C$$; weak acid $$CH_3COOH$$: $$[H^+] = \sqrt{K_a C}$$. $$K_w = 10^{-14}$$ links $$K_a$$ and $$K_b$$: $$K_w = K_a K_b$$.

nodes.label: Buffer Solutions
nodes.note: A weak acid plus its conjugate base resists pH change; Henderson-Hasselbalch: $$pH = pK_a + \log\frac{[\text{salt}]}{[\text{acid}]}$$. Blood ($$H_2CO_3/HCO_3^-$$) is the classic biological buffer.

nodes.label: Salt Hydrolysis
nodes.note: Salts of weak acid + strong base give basic solutions ($$CH_3COONa$$, $$pH > 7$$): $$CH_3COO^- + H_2O \rightleftharpoons CH_3COOH + OH^-$$. Salt of strong acid + weak base gives $$pH < 7$$ ($$NH_4Cl$$); weak+weak depends on $$K_a$$ vs $$K_b$$.

nodes.label: Solubility Product Ksp
nodes.note: For $$MX_2(s) \rightleftharpoons M^{2+} + 2X^-$$, $$K_{sp} = [M^{2+}][X^-]^2 = 4s^3$$. Precipitation starts when ionic product $$Q > K_{sp}$$; common ion effect suppresses solubility - basis of Group I/II cation separation.

nodes.label: Redox Reactions
nodes.note: Pillar chapter: Redox Reactions. Collects its JEE Main subtopics, trends and named tests in one branch.

nodes.label: Oxidation Number Rules
nodes.note: Rules: free element 0, $$O$$ is $$-2$$ (except peroxides $$-1$$, $$OF_2$$ $$+2$$), $$H$$ is $$+1$$ (except hydrides $$-1$$), sum equals charge. $$K_2Cr_2O_7$$: Cr is $$+6$$; $$H_2SO_5$$: one peroxy O pair makes S $$+6$$.

nodes.label: Oxidising and Reducing Agents
nodes.note: Oxidiser gains electrons (is reduced); reducer loses electrons (is oxidised). $$KMnO_4, K_2Cr_2O_7, HNO_3$$ are common oxidisers; $$Zn, NaBH_4, H_2S$$ are common reducers. Disproportionation: same species oxidised and reduced, e.g. $$Cl_2 + 2NaOH \rightarrow NaCl + NaClO + H_2O$$.

nodes.label: Balancing Redox (Ion-Electron)
